title: Board Regular Meeting Pt.2
overview: The Marathon County Board met to address the Hub City Wind project resolution from the Executive Committee, which lacked a concrete 'therefore be it resolved' clause. After extensive debate, the board voted to refer the matter back to the Executive Committee for a clearer recommendation, with supervisors expressing frustration over procedural issues and the county's limited authority to constrain the project given state PSC jurisdiction over large wind projects.

discussions.item: Hub City Wind Project Resolution – Procedural Objection
discussions.body: Vice Chair Chris Dickinson raised an immediate procedural objection, arguing the resolution was invalid because it contained no 'therefore be it resolved' clause — effectively resolving nothing. Corp Counsel confirmed the resolution was intentionally written that way to allow the board to amend it in whatever direction they chose. Dickinson called this unprecedented in his experience and expressed concern about setting a bad procedural precedent.

discussions.item: Motion to Refer Back to Executive Committee
discussions.body: Dickinson moved to refer the matter back to the Executive Committee to develop a concrete recommendation and bring it to the September board meeting. Supervisor Caravelli supported the referral, noting the item had been confusing even at the Thursday discussion. Vice Chair Boots explained she had brought it to the full board so all 38 supervisors could weigh in, but expressed no objection to referring it back.

discussions.item: Robinson Amendment (Not Voted On)
discussions.body: Supervisor Robinson described a proposed amendment that would direct the County Administrator to send Alliant Energy the Alternative Energy Project Local Impact Advisory Committee report and request a contractual response addressing community concerns by October 1st. Corp Counsel ruled this amendment was not germane to the motion to refer and therefore out of order while the referral motion was on the floor. Robinson noted the 180-day PSC application window made timely action important.

discussions.item: Moratorium Debate and PSC Jurisdiction
discussions.body: Multiple supervisors including Gaul, Hagan, Hopper, and Sendelbach advocated for a moratorium, citing constituent demand and the project's unprecedented tower height of 620 feet. Corp Counsel and Rebecca (a PSC representative on the line) clarified repeatedly that while the county could legally pass a moratorium, the PSC is not required to consider it for projects over 100 MW, rendering it largely symbolic. Supervisor Gaul pushed for the board to investigate formal intervention in the PSC process as an alternative approach.

discussions.item: Vote to End Debate and Refer to Executive Committee
discussions.body: Supervisor Ritter called the previous question, which was seconded by Supervisor Krebs. The motion to end debate passed, though not unanimously. The board then voted on the referral motion, which also carried but was not unanimous. The matter will return to the Executive Committee for a recommendation before coming back to the full board.

publicComment: No public comment was offered during this portion of the meeting, though supervisors referenced extensive prior public input with multiple speakers noting that over 90% of constituents at prior meetings opposed the Hub City Wind project or a joint development agreement with Alliant Energy.

title: Human Resources, Finances & Property Committee Meeting
committee: Marathon County Human Resources, Finances & Property Committee
overview: The Marathon County Human Resources, Finances & Property Committee met to address several action items and budget planning updates. Key decisions included tabling a WPS easement at Sunnyville Park for closed-session valuation negotiations, approving an amended donation acceptance policy requiring administrator acceptance with committee ratification at next meeting, and advancing a County Trunk Highway X developer cost-sharing agreement to the full county board. The committee also received an advisory presentation on an incoming conduit financing request from Wausau Hotel Group LLC for $10 million.

discussions.item: Approval of August 12th Minutes
discussions.body: Supervisor Hart moved to approve the August 12th minutes; Vice Chair Pool seconded. There was no discussion and the motion carried. The committee noted that joint meeting minutes with the EDC had not yet been approved and would be addressed at a future meeting.

discussions.item: 2027 Budget Development Update
discussions.body: County Administrator (Lance, based on context) provided a detailed budget update, noting that compensation and health insurance increases were funded first through a prioritization exercise, allowing departments to focus on holding operations flat. Staff reported that plow blade costs had increased from $300,000 to $600,000 year-over-year, approaching 300% over three years. A $125,000 hole in the District Attorney's office budget was noted due to the State Public Defender unilaterally reducing discovery fee payments. Key budget dates were outlined: budget delivery to committee September 29 at 1:00 p.m., publication approval October 14, public hearing November 2, committee amendment review November 9, and county board adoption November 10. A Wisconsin Counties Association Forward Analytics report was cited showing cumulative CPI rose 49.9% since 2010 while net new construction value rose only 24.1% statewide, underscoring fiscal constraints.

discussions.item: WPS Easement at Sunnyville Park
discussions.body: Vice Chair Chris Dickinson presented the WPS request for a natural gas regulator station easement in the northeast corner of Sunnyville Park, roughly three-quarters of an acre, with WPS offering $6,000. The Park Commission had conditionally recommended approval pending landscaping, color, and fencing requirements. Supervisor Gibbs raised concerns that the easement effectively renders the corner unusable and questioned whether the $6,000 reflects fair value, particularly given an adjacent gas line easement further limiting the land. Gibbs moved to postpone for a closed session to discuss negotiation strategy; the motion was seconded and carried unanimously, with the item expected to return in October.

discussions.item: 2027 Capital Improvement Budget Planning Strategy
discussions.body: This item had been placed on the agenda but no presentation or materials were prepared. Chair Robinson acknowledged the county is underfunding its capital improvement plan and deferring maintenance, referencing the jail and library situations as cautionary examples. The item was withdrawn from consideration at this meeting with no action taken.

discussions.item: Claim Disallowance – Hanky/Hunky Lawsuit
discussions.body: Corporation counsel advised that insurance-appointed legal counsel recommended formally disallowing the Hanky (also referenced as Hunky) claim on the basis that proper notice of claim was not provided by the claimant. A supervisor moved to deny the claim; Dave seconded. The motion carried with no opposition.

discussions.item: Resolution 5B1: Marathon County Donation Policy
discussions.body: The policy had been referred back from the county board following concerns from Supervisor Jensen about keeping donation acceptance within a board function rather than delegating fully to the administrator. Supervisor Jensen favored routing donations through this committee for approval; Supervisor Hart agreed and preferred quarterly reporting to this committee over full board reporting. Chair Gibbs moved an amendment allowing the administrator to provisionally accept donations consistent with policy, contingent on ratification by the HR Finance and Property Committee at its next meeting; Hart seconded. The amended motion carried. The item was then pulled from the evening county board agenda to allow staff time to draft clean amended language, with the intent to bring it back in September.

discussions.item: County Trunk Highway X Developer's Agreement
discussions.body: Highway Commissioner Kevin presented a cost-sharing agreement with a trucking facility developer (represented by Dave Hall of Rudabush) requiring year-round truck access along County Road X due to a restriction on Business 51 prohibiting trucks over 65 feet. The developer agreed to fund 50% of an estimated $700,000 structural overlay on Highway X and 75% of an estimated $113,000 intersection reconstruction at County Road X and Double X, plus 100% of right-of-way and engineering costs. The county would purchase the full outlot at the northeast corner for future use, with the developer funding 10% of that acquisition cost. A cancellation clause requires the developer to reimburse county expenditures if they cancel. Infrastructure Committee had previously reviewed and directed staff on this approach. Vice Chair Pool moved to recommend approval and advance to the county board; Gibbs seconded. Motion carried unanimously.

discussions.item: Conduit Financing – Wausau Hotel Group LLC (Informational)
discussions.body: The administrator provided an advance notice that Wausau Hotel Group LLC is seeking $10 million in conduit financing through the Public Finance Authority. Under county ordinance section 1.51(7), this committee must evaluate and recommend to the full board; the administrator alone cannot consent. The financing would not pledge the county's faith and credit and is not an endorsement of the project. The representative confirmed the September 17th county board meeting timeline is acceptable, so the item will formally appear at the committee's first September meeting. Supervisor Jensen raised a question about whether the ordinance's bond duration limits apply; the administrator committed to researching that for the next meeting.

title: Finance Committee Meeting
overview: The Wausau Finance Committee met on August 25, 2026, approving several personnel and financial items including a planning intern position for the comprehensive plan update, reclassification of an HR specialist to generalist (with one dissenting vote), a 2026 budget calendar, and a tax increment revenue bond for the Foundry on Third development. The committee also held extended discussions on lead service line replacement funding gaps, the city's 2026 general obligation promissory note sale results, equalized and assessed property values, and a review of 2025 financial results.

discussions.item: Approval of creation of planning intern position
discussions.body: Community Development Director Carrie Edmonson presented the request for a temporary part-time planning intern to assist with public engagement for the mandatory comprehensive plan update, funded through an existing capital request with no additional budget impact. Alder Watson asked about funding sources and was told costs are covered through the comprehensive plan capital allocation. Alder Hincki raised concerns about whether an inexperienced intern could handle difficult public conversations; Edmonson clarified the intern would never conduct public engagement alone and would always work alongside experienced staff. Alder Neil asked about the ideal skill set, and Edmonson indicated UWSP students in land resources or planning would be the likely target pool. The item had previously passed unanimously at the HR Committee.

discussions.item: Approval of reclassification of HR Specialist to HR Generalist
discussions.body: Interim HR Director Ann Keenan presented the reclassification, noting the current specialist has been performing full generalist duties since the city moved to a two-person HR staff with Workday implementation, and faces a heavy workload including nine apprentice hires, police deputy recruitment, ADA compliance items, FMLA, and worker's comp. Alder Hincki expressed concern that the proposed pay range (up to the high $70s) exceeded what he found on Indeed and Glassdoor for the local market, though Keenan noted Marathon County's generalist pay aligns with the proposed range. Chair Martins argued it was inequitable to have someone doing generalist work capped at a specialist pay grade. Hincki voted no, with the motion passing over his dissent.

discussions.item: Establishing 2026 budget calendar dates
discussions.body: Finance Director Maryanne [last name not stated] presented four proposed budget workshop dates starting October 5, with sessions set at 6:30 p.m. to avoid conflicts with other committee meetings. She noted historical practice of canceling unneeded sessions. Alder Tierney emphasized she would not participate if budget books were not provided with ample advance notice, and abstained from the final vote. The calendar was approved with Tierney not voting.

discussions.item: Approval of Foundry on Third tax increment revenue bond
discussions.body: Economic Development Director Patrick [last name not stated] explained the municipal revenue obligation bond is required by the developer agreement with T-Wall as part of a pay-as-you-go TIF incentive structure, allowing the developer to show their lender a guarantee of future TIF payments. Finance staff clarified that the bond is backed by tax increment revenue from the district, not the general fund, and does not add to the city's general indebtedness. Alder Hincki asked about developer performance requirements and was told the developer is currently meeting minimum assessed value and construction cost thresholds in the agreement. The 2025 assessed value was $7.1 million and the 2026 value is $33.6 million. The motion was approved unanimously.

discussions.item: Discussion: options to pay for private-side lead service line replacement not covered by grants
discussions.body: City Engineer Eric [last name not stated] presented three options for covering the growing funding gap on private-side lead service line replacement as state and federal grant funds diminish. In 2026, the city covered approximately $3.3 million of the private-side funding gap. Alder Hincki expressed concern about equity between residents whose lines were replaced earlier at no cost versus those who may face charges later, and asked whether costs could be spread via special assessment over 10 years. Alder Watson asked about income-based or property-value-based subsidies rather than a flat dollar amount, and whether costs could be expressed as a percentage rather than a fixed sum. Alder Neil suggested accelerating replacements to take advantage of current lower costs and the expiring 0.25% loan rate in 2027. The discussion touched on potential use of TIF excess funds but noted council had previously removed lead service line language from multiple TID project plan amendments. No action was taken; the discussion will continue during the 2027 budget process.

discussions.item: Presentation from Ehlers regarding 2026A promissory note sale
discussions.body: Brian Rohr from Ehlers reported that the city's $10,560,000 general obligation promissory note sale in June received seven bids — described as extraordinary — with a low-to-high spread of only 17 basis points, indicating strong market demand. The notes closed July 9 at approximately 3.1% interest, saving about $52,000-$53,000 versus estimates. Moody's affirmed the city's Aa3 rating. The resulting debt adds about $382,000 to the 2027 debt levy, representing roughly a $6 change on a $350,000 property's tax bill. The city's general obligation debt stands at approximately 31% of its statutory 5% equalized value limit, with $164 million in remaining capacity. Alder Hincki asked about debt per capita comparisons with peer communities; Rohr agreed to provide that data. Finance Director Maryanne emphasized the city retires debt faster than most peers, using 10-year or shorter amortization schedules.

discussions.item: Presentation on equalized and assessed valuation and role within budget
discussions.body: Finance Director Maryanne delivered an educational presentation explaining Wisconsin's dual-value assessment system, levy limits tied to net new construction, expenditure restraint program incentives ($1.3 million grant received in 2026), and how TID closures affect levy capacity. She noted the city is now at 8.34% of its TID equalized value limit, well below the 12% cap, after recent district closures. Alder Hincki asked whether the city has policies against using long-term debt for operating expenses; Maryanne confirmed state rules effectively prevent this by requiring debt to match asset life. She also clarified that the firefighter referendum positions were successfully incorporated within the expenditure restraint program over three years, avoiding repayment obligations to the state.

discussions.item: Presentation on 2025 financial results
discussions.body: Rather than a full slide-by-slide walkthrough, Chair Martins and Alder Neil agreed the lengthy presentation would be deferred largely to questions, noting much of the content had been covered in earlier presentations. Maryanne indicated auditors are wrapping up the single audit and will present formally at a September regular meeting date to be determined. Alder Neil asked candidly whether the city's financial health is deteriorating, improving, or static; Maryanne indicated she had addressed comparative data in the presentation but the full answer was cut off in the transcript.

title: Board Regular Meeting Pt.1
overview: The Marathon County Board of Supervisors held its regular meeting on August 25, covering several significant items including a contested infrastructure committee chair appointment, amendments to battery energy storage and large energy facility ordinances, a data center moratorium, and a pivotal vote on whether to proceed with Phase 3 of a new county highway facility estimated to potentially cost up to $60 million. The meeting was significant for residents as it set new zoning rules for battery storage systems, established a temporary moratorium on data centers, and moved the controversial highway garage project forward toward competitive bidding.

discussions.body: Motion by Supervisor Rosenberg, seconded by Supervisor Jeang. Supervisor Arstead requested C11A be pulled for a separate vote. A supervisor also briefly confused this agenda block with Resolution 49-26 (highway facility), which Chair Gibbs clarified was a separate item. The remaining consent agenda passed unanimously.

discussions.item: C11A - Infrastructure Committee Chair Appointment
discussions.body: The contested appointment pitted Supervisor Griner (a second-term supervisor) against Supervisor Gao (a first-term supervisor serving as vice chair of infrastructure). Supervisor Arstead argued Gao had proven himself through his response to the Ringle tornado and his experience as a supervisor in Dane County. Vice Chair Dickinson echoed support for Gao, noting Gao had chaired meetings in Dickinson's absence and was more experienced overall. Chair Gibbs and Vice Chair Boots defended Griner, citing a tradition of not placing first-term supervisors as committee chairs. Supervisor Drebeck suggested the matter go to the Rules Review Committee in the future. The motion to approve Griner as Infrastructure Committee chair failed, and Gibbs said he and the vice chair would meet to recommend a chair for next month.

discussions.item: Ordinance 27-26 - Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) Amendment
discussions.body: Staff planner Shad Harvey presented the ordinance as strengthening existing Chapter 17 BESS protections. Supervisor Dickinson raised the question of whether the 300-foot residential setback was adequate given ember travel in fires, and staff recommended 500 feet as a defensible middle ground. Supervisor Sundoski moved to refer the ordinance back to the Environmental Resources Committee (ERC) citing concerns about missing provisions on waterways, decommissioning, and liability; this motion was seconded by Supervisor Hapa but failed on a vote. Supervisor Dickinson then moved to amend the setback from 300 to 500 feet, and Supervisor Sundoski moved a further amendment to extend that setback to all structures, not just residences. Both amendments passed. The ordinance as twice-amended was then approved, though not unanimously. Staff clarified that standalone BESS under county zoning require conditional use permits reviewed by the Board of Adjustment, and system owners are required to provide and replace specialized firefighting equipment for first responders.

discussions.item: Ordinance 28-26 - Moratorium on Data Centers
discussions.body: Motion by Supervisor Drebeck, seconded by Supervisor Conway. Chair Gibbs noted the county currently has no Chapter 17 provisions for data centers, and the moratorium of up to 12 months gives staff time to develop an ordinance. No significant debate was recorded. The ordinance passed but was not unanimous.

discussions.item: Ordinance 29-26 - Large Energy Generating Facilities Amendment
discussions.body: This novel ordinance — described by outside counsel Rebecca Roker as the first of its kind in Wisconsin — would require developers to submit engineering plans to the county 60 days before filing a CPCN application with the PSC, giving the county an early engagement opportunity. Supervisor Leur expressed concern about vague, unmeasurable language in sections 3 and 4 regarding 'undue adverse impact' and 'unreasonably interfere.' Supervisor Sundoski moved to refer back to ERC for consideration of a moratorium; that motion failed. Supervisor Dickinson then moved to amend the ordinance to require the county to share received engineering plan information with all municipalities in Marathon County, seconded by Supervisor Arstead; that amendment passed unanimously. The ordinance as amended was then approved, though not unanimously. Supervisor Gao cautioned that vague moratorium language would be dismissed by the PSC.

discussions.item: Resolution 49-26 (E18) - Phase 3 Construction of New Highway Facility
discussions.body: Supervisor Krebs gave a lengthy statement opposing the project on fiscal grounds, comparing the potential $55-60 million price tag unfavorably to a fire station, police department, and DPW garage combined, and calling for a public referendum. Supervisors Robinson, Dickinson, Griner, Ness, and Vice Chair Boots defended the resolution, emphasizing it only authorizes staff to release bid documents to obtain a guaranteed maximum price — not to break ground — and that construction costs continue to rise annually. Concerns were raised about coal dust from the adjacent WPS plant affecting employee health; staff noted HVAC filtration is designed to address particulate matter and WPS is expected to transition from coal to natural gas by the early 2030s. Administrator Leonard confirmed the resolution accomplishes two things: authorizing bid release and approving a general financial plan using previously issued debt to reduce new borrowing needs. The vote outcome was not explicitly stated in the transcript before the recording ended.

discussions.item: Welcome of New Commissioner Lisa Nowak and Appointment of Secretary
discussions.body: The commission president welcomed Lisa Nowak as the newest member, filling the seat vacated by Cheryl Barr, with a term ending April 30, 2028. Her HR background was cited as an asset. The president also announced the appointment of V Lesky as commission secretary, citing his legal background, to fill the vacancy left by Cheryl Barr's retirement from the commission.

discussions.body: The commission president noted that the June 22nd minutes were returning for correction — a date error listed 'April 2026' had been corrected to 'April 2025' in reference to when a complaint started. A motion was made to approve all three sets of minutes together; it was seconded and passed unanimously with no objection.

discussions.item: Discussion and Possible Action on Deputy Chief Promotional Process
discussions.body: The commission president outlined a new, more robust internal deputy chief promotional process developed collaboratively with the police chief, framed as an early step in chief succession planning given that the deputy chief is retiring in January 2027 and the chief intends to retire in early 2028. The process would include listening sessions with officers, detectives, clerical staff, and lieutenants; formal candidate presentations to the commission on financial and operational challenges; written department assessments; panel interviews; and the chief's one-on-one interviews before making a final recommendation. Commissioners expressed general support, with one asking whether public participation should be incorporated; the president suggested that level of public involvement may be more appropriate at the chief selection stage. The chief suggested that annual listening sessions with staff could benefit the commission's ongoing understanding of department culture. The commission agreed to proceed, targeting applications in September, screening in November, and a decision at the December PFC meeting. A commissioner flagged that a special December meeting may be needed given potential overlap with a police hiring process.

discussions.item: Fire Department Monthly Update (Chief Cobb)
discussions.body: Fire Chief Cobb reported that the apprenticeship program is on track with 45 applicants for nine positions, led by Deputy Chief Ploussard in partnership with NTC. However, the department remains six positions down with another retirement in December. One of two candidates from a prior special meeting failed the psychological exam and will not advance; the other is awaiting a physical agility test delayed by a broken stair stepper at NTC. The chief also noted significant budget pressure, with direction from the mayor's office to cut approximately 2% from the budget, requiring creative solutions alongside Deputy Chief.

discussions.item: Police Department Monthly Update (Chief Barnes)
discussions.body: Chief Barnes described a difficult recent period including a use-of-force incident that went viral on social media, generating hundreds of critical emails, as well as a fatal fire and multiple death-related calls affecting officer mental health. The department has three current openings and anticipates six retirements in early 2027, creating a need to hire nine officers — historically difficult in a single process. The chief said 22 candidates are currently in the queue with the application period still open. He explained the complexity of the state's maintenance-of-effort requirement tied to shared revenue, noting that the penalty for falling short far exceeds the ~$300,000 in budget cuts being requested. He expressed optimism about 2027 and mentioned a fundraiser for 24-year-old Officer Rafael 'Buddy' Carey, who is battling stage four cancer. The commission president suggested adding the annual report to the next agenda for further questions.

title: Board of Trustees and Finance/HR
overview: The Village of Weston Board of Trustees and Finance/HR Committee held a joint budget workshop — the first such joint meeting in several years — focused on educating board members about governmental fund accounting, reviewing equalized values and levy limits for the 2027 budget cycle, and beginning preliminary budget discussions. Key decisions included approving a $1.29 million waterworks revenue bond for a water system project and voting to keep trustee compensation unchanged for the 2027–2029 term at $7,200 for trustees and $8,400 for the village president.

discussions.item: Resolution 2026-023: Waterworks Revenue Bonds
discussions.body: The board approved a resolution authorizing the issuance of up to $1,291,283 in waterworks system revenue bonds. Staff explained that the broader project totals approximately $4.3 million but the village received roughly $3 million in principal forgiveness through a state safe drinking water loan, and an additional $272,460 was removed from the project amount due to PFAS class action lawsuit proceeds. The interest rate on the borrowing is 0.365% with total interest of approximately $333,000. The motion was approved unanimously by the board; the Finance/HR committee did not vote separately as staff confirmed this was a board-only item.

discussions.item: Governmental Fund Accounting and Budget Process Presentation
discussions.body: Finance Director Jessica provided an extensive educational presentation on governmental fund accounting, covering the general fund, special revenue funds, debt service, capital projects, and proprietary/enterprise funds for water, sewer, and storm. She explained the modified accrual basis of accounting, why long-term liabilities and receivables such as the Mountain Bay repayment do not appear on fund balance sheets in the traditional sense, and the distinction between the capital improvement program and the capital projects fund. Village President Maloney noted the timeline requires budget adoption at the November board meeting to meet county tax bill printing deadlines.

discussions.item: Levy Limits, Equalized Value, and Net New Construction
discussions.body: Staff presented the state's August 11 equalized value report showing the village's net new construction at approximately $31.3 million, representing a 1.624% increase — the maximum allowable levy increase for 2027. The village's total equalized value change was 9%. Staff noted that fixed cost increases such as a workers' compensation modifier increase from 0.86 to 1.17 (a roughly $30,000 hit), Mountain Bay cost increases, and stagnant state aids like cable franchise fees and personal property aid effectively consume most or all of the allowable levy increase before any discretionary spending decisions are made. Staff also flagged uncertainty around how the TIF 2 closure — expected to yield roughly $400,000 in additional levy capacity — will be treated by the state on the levy limit worksheet.

discussions.item: Expenditure Restraint Program
discussions.body: Staff explained the village currently receives $138,000 under the state expenditure restraint program — $88,000 in the general fund and $50,000 in capital — and expressed concern that the TIF 2 closure could push general fund expenditures above program thresholds and disqualify the village. A potential strategy discussed was moving general transportation aid and associated street maintenance expenditures out of the general fund into Fund 42 to keep general fund expenditures within restraint limits. Staff acknowledged the rules have significant complexity and work-arounds but emphasized compliance.

discussions.item: 2027 Budget Priorities Discussion
discussions.body: Trustees debated whether the stated budget priorities aligned with community priorities identified in the comprehensive plan, where road maintenance (86% importance, 13% satisfaction) and public safety topped the list. Trustee Clark questioned whether items like a robotic lawnmower reflected village priorities or staff wish-list items, and suggested reframing such items around staff retention and reallocation rather than equipment purchases. Trustee Ermeling and others raised the process concern that discussing wages before knowing available revenues was backwards. A citizen Finance/HR committee member requested data on the number of employees at various pay ranges, supervisor-to-employee compression, merit pay examples, and the total all-in cost per 1% salary change. Staff confirmed SAFER-funded firefighters (approximately 68% of their cost) would migrate to the general fund upon program transition, representing a significant budget pressure.

discussions.item: Wages, Benefits, and Health Insurance Update
discussions.body: Staff reported that Spectrum (the village's health insurance consortium) has preliminarily estimated a 15% premium increase for 2027, though last year's preliminary estimate of 20% came in at negative 5%. The budget currently carries a 10% placeholder. Staff will conduct a form-fire analysis to price the village independently as a contingency. A 3% COLA placeholder has been included for staff wages along with a merit and market component. The average hourly wage is approximately $63,382 and average salary is approximately $88,724, with the highest salary at $127,000. Trustees discussed alternatives to straight percentage raises including HSA contribution increases, additional holidays (Martin Luther King Day, Juneteenth, Veterans Day), and 4x10 work schedules. The village has an 85/15 premium split with employees and has absorbed premium increases the past two years without passing costs to employees.

discussions.item: Trustee Compensation for 2027–2029 Term
discussions.body: Village President Maloney stated he did not believe trustee compensation needed to change, noting trustees earn $7,200 per year and the president earns $8,400 — rates set approximately eight years ago after 24 years with no adjustment. He cited comparators including the Town of Weston chair at $14,000, the City of Schofield at $12,000–$13,000, and Marathon County supervisors at $4,600. The Finance/HR committee moved and seconded to leave compensation unchanged for the 2027–2029 term; the motion carried. The full board then made the same motion, which also passed unanimously.

discussions.item: Capital Improvement Plan Review
discussions.body: Staff reviewed the 2026–2027 capital improvement fund accounts covering facilities, streets, and equipment. Most 2026 projects are already underway with engineering and contracts in place. A $1 million line item for the Howland project was identified as a coding error — correctly budgeted but placed under 'workers comp' rather than 'contracted services/street and curb.' A $100,000 placeholder was included for pool leak detection, described as a rough estimate pending ongoing exploration. Staff confirmed no capital expenditures move forward without final board approval regardless of CIP inclusion.

Most critically, he argued that discussing pay increases as the first budget item was premature and inappropriate given that revenue figures and mandated costs are not yet known, and that citizen-identified priorities like public safety and streets should come first.

title: City Council Rules Review Committee Meeting
committee: Wausau City Council Rules Review Committee
overview: The Wausau City Council Rules Review Committee met to examine possible language changes regarding how all committee personnel are selected. The committee's scope was clarified as limited to Chapter 216 (common council rules), not commissions or bodies like the ethics board. The committee approved one concrete rule change: amending Rule 13D so that subcommittee and special committee chairpersons are elected by majority vote of the subcommittee at the start of the term, rather than being named by the standing committee chairperson.

discussions.item: Parliamentarian overview of Rule 13A and appointment process
discussions.body: The city's parliamentarian explained that Rule 13A states the mayor shall appoint members to standing committees at the organizational meeting, but provides no further guidance. He noted that appointment processes for other bodies are generally specified in the ordinance or resolution creating the committee, or by statute for commissions. He confirmed that alderpersons may decline appointments, leaving the position vacant for the mayor to fill again.

discussions.item: Alderperson ability to decline or step down from committee assignments
discussions.body: Alder Watson raised the difficulty of declining scheduling-incompatible assignments in a formal way. Alder Killian said she had always felt comfortable communicating with the mayor and felt the current process worked, though she acknowledged scheduling could be challenging for those with regular employment. The parliamentarian confirmed no rule requires acceptance of an appointment and suggested spelling this out in the rules would be helpful. The chair noted she had personally stepped down from a committee mid-term in a prior session and that this informal process had worked, but that midterm vacancies are not currently addressed in writing.

discussions.item: Amendment to Rule 13D — subcommittee chairperson election process
discussions.body: Alder Killian raised that a controversy arose this term over the bike and pedestrian subcommittee chair, where members were surprised to learn the infrastructure committee chair had authority to appoint the subcommittee chair rather than the subcommittee electing its own. Alder Watson moved to amend Rule 13D to strike the sentence giving the standing committee chairperson power to name subcommittee chairs and replace it with language requiring the subcommittee or special committee to elect its own chairperson by majority vote at the start of the term. After discussion refining the language, the amendment passed unanimously, as did the underlying amended motion. The amendment will go to the full council, where a two-thirds vote is required to amend the rules.

discussions.item: Scope of rules review committee and citizen/ethics board appointments
discussions.body: The chair raised whether the impetus for the meeting — a challenge by Alderpersons Lucans and Larson related to an ethics committee appointment — could be addressed by the rules committee. The parliamentarian clarified the committee's resolution limits its scope to Chapter 216, the common council's standing rules, and does not extend to ethics board appointments (governed by a separate ordinance, Chapter 203) or to commissions governed by state statute. Alder Watson asked whether amendments to other chapters were possible but was informed those fall outside this committee's purview.

discussions.item: Clarification on committees vs. commissions
discussions.body: The parliamentarian explained the distinction between commissions (created by state statute, with composition and appointment rules dictated by the legislature, such as the police and fire commission and transit commission) and committees or boards (created by the council, with more flexibility in how they are composed and governed). Standing committee chairs, with two exceptions — transit (governed by statute) and rules review (appointed by mayor per the creating resolution) — are elected by committee members, not appointed by the mayor.

publicComment: No public comment was offered. The chair opened the floor for public comment and, seeing no members of the public present, closed the public comment period.
actionItems: Amended Rule 13D — striking language giving standing committee chairs power to name subcommittee chairs and replacing it with a requirement that subcommittees and special committees elect their own chairperson by majority vote at the start of the term — to be forwarded to the full City Council for a two-thirds vote.

A generator battery failure was discovered and addressed in-house, with discussion about the aging generator fleet and the need for a long-term replacement plan.

discussions.body: Finance Director John Jacobs reported the general fund revenues are tracking nearly identically to 2025 at about 62.7% collected through seven months, with most remaining revenue expected from the state in October. Three expenditure areas flagged as over budget - legal/investigation costs, municipal building operations, and garbage/recycling - are expected to be addressed via a transfer from the $60,000 contingency reserve later in the year. On TID #1, Jacobs explained a combined $2.5 million valuation reduction resulted from local assessor adjustments and a retroactive state correction, worsening the TID's cash flow. He recommended a status quo approach for six to nine months to allow a potential distribution center project to add tax increment, noting debt payments drop significantly starting in 2030 and TID #1 debt is eliminated by 2037-2044.

discussions.body: Finance Director Jacobs and Public Works Director Greg presented the 10-year CIP, noting the village currently has roughly $49 million in remaining borrowing capacity at 70% of the debt limit. Trustee Erin Mishka (Parks Committee Chair) specifically noted that the $200,000 in park donations listed for 2027 is insufficient and that tax dollars should support parks improvements. title: Board Educational Meeting Pt.2
overview: The Marathon County Board held a lengthy educational meeting reviewing upcoming voting items including zoning ordinance amendments for battery energy storage systems, a data center moratorium, and a large electric generating facility ordinance. The board also received an extensive briefing on plans for a new county highway facility estimated at $50-55 million, with staff presenting a financing strategy using existing debt and North Central Healthcare revenues to avoid new long-term borrowing. No binding votes were taken as this was an educational/review session ahead of the formal voting meeting.

discussions.item: Appointment of Aaron Griner as Infrastructure Committee Chair
discussions.body: Supervisor Arstead questioned why the committee's vice chair was passed over for the chair position, noting that prior practice had been for the vice chair to assume the role when a chair vacates. Chair Gibbs explained that he and Vice Chair Dickinson reviewed supervisors by tenure and recommended Griner. Supervisor Robinson asked whether a new vice chair would be designated; Gibbs confirmed the existing vice chair remains in place.

discussions.item: Battery Energy Storage Systems Ordinance (0-27-26)
discussions.body: Zoning Administrator Shad Harvey explained the ordinance updates an existing BEST chapter to add emergency response plan requirements, first responder training and PPE obligations, system owner liability for EMS costs, and clearer decommissioning standards. Supervisor Sundowski announced he planned to offer two amendments at the voting meeting: an 1,800-foot setback from dwellings and waterways, and a secondary concrete containment requirement. Harvey cautioned that an 1,800-foot setback would effectively prohibit BEST systems in Marathon County given its wetlands, and questioned whether rigid secondary containment could interfere with manufacturer safety requirements. Supervisor Gao raised concerns about distinguishing residential from commercial BEST systems and appropriate setbacks for larger systems above 5 megawatts. Supervisor Ritter argued the ordinance should be passed now and amended later as more information becomes available; Gao agreed. The board reached consensus to move forward.

discussions.item: Data Center Moratorium Ordinance (0-28-26)
discussions.body: Harvey explained the proposed 12-month moratorium would allow the county to develop a zoning ordinance for data centers, as none currently exists. Supervisor Gao cautioned that public perception of the moratorium as an outright ban on data centers is inaccurate, stating the moratorium only provides time to draft regulations. Supervisor Leur clarified the moratorium applies only to county-zoned towns, not incorporated municipalities or unzoned townships.

discussions.item: Large Electric Generating Facility Ordinance (0-29-26)
discussions.body: Harvey explained that because Wisconsin Statute 196.401 grants the PSC authority over facilities over 100 megawatts once a CPCN is issued, the county cannot regulate such facilities directly. The ordinance is designed to strengthen county notification within the PSC process so the board can decide whether to intervene. Supervisor Gao strongly supported the ordinance, noting the Town of Easton situation as an example where a solar farm proceeded without the county board having any advance information.

discussions.item: Parks Department Fee Ordinance (0-30-26)
discussions.body: County Administrator Leonard requested that the ordinance be pulled from the voting agenda, explaining that a broader review of all county ordinances containing fee references is needed to eliminate conflicts between ordinances and the fee schedule. Leonard's goal is to remove specific dollar amounts from ordinances and replace them with references to the fee schedule, with a target of completing that review within a month. The board indicated a committee member would formally move to pull Ordinance 0-30-26 at the voting meeting.

discussions.item: Highway Facility Phase 3 Resolution (Resolution 49-26)
discussions.body: Staff presented a two-part resolution: directing finalization of design and release of bid documents to determine actual cost of the new highway facility (previously estimated at $50-55 million), and directing staff to build the 2027 budget around a financing strategy that shifts North Central Healthcare debt service revenues to a project fund rather than issuing new long-term bonds. Financial advisor Kristen Hansen reported current municipal bond rates at approximately 4.16-4.17% for 20-year general obligation notes, compared to the county's existing debt issued at roughly 1.2-3.8%. Administrator Leonard explained the strategy avoids new 20-year borrowing by transitioning existing debt to debt levy over roughly two years and accumulating North Central Healthcare revenues over six to seven years. The highway fund balance totals approximately $79.4 million, of which $30 million is reserved for the highway shop, leaving only $91,000 truly unallocated. Supervisors questioned phased construction, staging of the West Street facility divestment, and contingency plans if North Central Healthcare revenues fall short. The City of Wausau has expressed interest in the West Street property.

discussions.item: Tattoo and Piercing Fee Schedule (Resolution 53-26)
discussions.body: Administrator Leonard and Health Department representative Kate Floric explained that the county's interpretation of DSPS regulations requires licensing each individual practitioner area separately at temporary events, which organizers of the Cedar Creek Inkfest convention argued would be costly. Staff proposed a tiered fee structure allowing up to six practitioners to share one license. Supervisor Pool proposed amending the resolution to delay the effective date until after the mid-October Cedar Creek Inkfest event to avoid disrupting the organizers on short notice. Supervisor Mash expressed support for Pool's proposal, and Administrator Leonard agreed staff would meet with event organizers to clarify how many shops would be involved and how the existing versus proposed fee structure would apply to them.

No public speakers addressed the board during this session.

title: Board Educational Meeting Pt.1
overview: The Marathon County Board of Supervisors held an educational meeting focused primarily on the Hub City Wind project and options available to the county, featuring extensive public comment overwhelmingly opposed to a Joint Development Agreement (JDA) with Alliant Energy, followed by legal presentations from attorneys Rebecca Roker and Bill Omin advising that a JDA is the county's best available tool given state preemption of local wind energy regulation. The meeting also included educational presentations on the NTC-UWSP partnership and an update on the Allison Dairland program. No formal votes were taken, as this was designated an educational meeting.

discussions.item: Public Comment – Hub City Wind and JDA
discussions.body: Fifteen of the seventeen public speakers addressed the Hub City Wind project, with the overwhelming majority urging the board not to enter into a Joint Development Agreement with Alliant Energy. Speakers including Joe Bergen (Town of Day), Tren Spindler (Town of Day, chair of an intergovernmental committee of five affected townships), Cindy Nelson (Town of Opa), Jackie Dillinger (Town of Day), Nikki Catrell (Brighton Township), and others argued the county should instead pursue a limited moratorium and/or intervene at the PSC. Multiple speakers cited the county's own public survey and alternative energy committee recommendation against a JDA. Becky Tyro criticized the alternative energy task force as having produced no meaningful action despite overwhelming public opposition. One speaker, Harry Turkington from Madison, spoke in favor of a well-negotiated JDA, citing Marathon County's projected 5.5% population loss by 2050 and potential revenue benefits.

discussions.item: Public Comment – Cedar Creek Incfest Body Art Convention Licensing Fees (Resolution R5326)
discussions.body: Three speakers addressed proposed resolution R5326 regarding temporary body art event licensing fees. Brandy Candenberg (Village of Maine), organizing Cedar Creek Incfest coming to Rothschild in October, asked the board to vote no as presented, citing that the fee structure — roughly $208 per license covering six practitioners — could cost her event up to $14,000, compared to $130 in Sauk County and under $150 in Portage and Wood counties. Dave Brua, tourism marketing director for the Village of Rothschild, noted the event is expected to draw 6,000 attendees with a projected $500,000 economic impact. Mark Hannenburg, a local tattoo shop owner helping organize the event, argued the fee structure creates a 'cliff' where one additional practitioner doubles the cost and called for a more defensible fee methodology.

discussions.item: Standing Committee Report – County Highway XX Developer Agreement and Related Items
discussions.body: Supervisor Chris Dickinson (appearing remotely, initially experiencing audio issues) reported on three related items: ordinance amendment 032-26 for a four-way stop on County Highway XX, resolution R4826 urging the state DOT to increase truck length allowances on Highway 51, and an upcoming developer agreement. He explained a new facility planned on County Highway XX and Trellwood Lane requires trucks over 65 feet, which are technically restricted from Business 51 under state code — a restriction not currently enforced but not legally resolved. Because the state will not act until at least January 2027 due to elections, the developer sought a county agreement providing a legal route via County Highway XX to allow construction to begin this fall for a 2028 opening. The agreement would have the developer fund 75% of an intersection improvement and 50% of resurfacing for 2.3 miles of County Highway X, with a cancellation clause protecting the county from costs if the state resolves the issue sooner.

discussions.item: Educational Presentation: NTC and UWSP 'Purple and Blue Advantage' Partnership
discussions.body: NTC COO Darren Ackley and UWSP Dean of University College Gretle Stock presented plans to collocate UWSP at Wausau on NTC's Wausau campus beginning fall 2026, creating a seamless two-to-four-year degree pathway. Key points included that NTC associate degree graduates in the region earn an average of $54,000 annually, while a combined NTC-to-UWSP bachelor's degree pathway costs students approximately $30,000 compared to $75,000–$106,000 at a traditional four-year residential institution. They noted that only 28% of central Wisconsin residents hold bachelor's degrees versus 38% nationally, and that the partnership would place advisers from both institutions side by side to guide students. The board received the presentation and Chair Gibbs thanked the presenters; no questions from the board were noted on the record.

discussions.item: Hub City Wind – Legal Presentation on County Options (Item 9C7A)
discussions.body: Attorneys Rebecca Roker (Atollus Law, appearing virtually) and Bill Omin (UW-Madison Extension Law Center) presented to the board on the county's legal options regarding Hub City Wind. Both attorneys confirmed that under Wisconsin statutes (Chapter 196 and Chapter 66) and existing PSC case law, Marathon County is substantially preempted from regulating large-scale renewable energy projects. Omin stated he reviewed all relevant PSC dockets and found no instance where a local government's intervention caused the PSC to deny a utility's project application. Roker described moratoriums as 'frowned upon' under Wisconsin law and legally risky if the motivation is to halt development. Both attorneys advised that a JDA represents the best available mechanism for the county to address resident concerns, noting it is a contract that can include provisions on noise, road repairs, decommissioning, payments in lieu of taxes, and mitigation of unanticipated damages — though the developer is not obligated to agree to any specific term. During board Q&A, Supervisor Rosenberg asked whether a trust fund for remediation could be negotiated; attorneys said it was possible to ask for but must be supported by data and is subject to negotiation. Supervisor Wilhelm asked whether a JDA would release Alliant from unforeseen liability; Roker said a properly drafted JDA would include provisions holding Alliant responsible. Supervisor Aaron Griner pressed on the extent to which the PSC is legally obligated to consider county input, and Roker acknowledged there is 'no legal standard for consider' within the statute and that PSC has no obligation to consider a moratorium at all.

publicComment: Seventeen speakers signed up; approximately 15 addressed the Hub City Wind project and the proposed JDA with Alliant Energy. Nearly all who spoke on that topic were opposed to entering a JDA and urged the board to pursue a limited moratorium and/or PSC intervention instead. Speakers cited the county's own public forum results, the alternative energy committee's recommendation against a JDA, concerns about turbine health impacts, property values, wildlife, airspace safety near private airstrips, and the lack of operating precedent for 680-foot turbines. One speaker (Harry Turkington, City of Madison) spoke in favor of a well-negotiated JDA citing demographic and fiscal concerns. Three speakers addressed resolution R5326 on body art convention licensing fees, urging the board to vote no on the current proposal and requesting a revised fee structure before adoption.

discussions.item: Public Comment – Seclusion Room at Evergreen Elementary
discussions.body: Mary Soulheim, a district resident and parent of students at Evergreen Elementary, addressed the board about behavioral intervention practices. She stated the district was found in direct violation of Wisconsin Statute 118.305 for maintaining a seclusion room with a locked door and hazards at Evergreen Elementary during the 2024-2025 school year. She described the room as a former storage closet measuring just over 4 by 6 feet, and argued that retrofitting it with padding and training staff to use it for seclusion would be traumatizing to students and shift school culture away from proactive mental health support. She urged the board to halt the rollout of the plan and direct administration to conduct a review of legal and psychological risks, proposing the topic be brought back in September.

discussions.item: CISA 9 Report and Commendation of Larry Schaefer
discussions.body: Larry Schaefer reported on the CISA 9 annual meeting, noting that Gary Moon from North Lakeland was elected as the large-district representative, ending Schaefer's tenure on the CISA 9 Board of Control after four years. Board President Shannon Grabko read aloud a commendation letter from CISA 9 administrator Al Betri praising Schaefer's service, leadership, and professionalism. Officer Matt Loveless described a four-day joint critical incident rescue task force training held at the middle school July 27-30, involving approximately 30 Mountain Bay Metro Police officers and 20 Riverside Fire District personnel, using student volunteers for realistic scenarios. Dr. Knight also reported that after a demo, the district decided not to implement a $4,000 AI chatbot from Final Site this year due to cost, quality concerns, and pending ADA compliance rules effective April 2026.

discussions.item: Summer School Report
discussions.body: Mike Rayther and Nikki Matthews presented the summer learning report in Rayther's first year leading the program. Highlights included an Engineering Tomorrow partnership with Greenheck on sound mitigation, strength and conditioning programming with CTI, a patriotic musical performance called 'America 250' involving about 70 students, the Hmong enrichment program co-run with Wausau School District and CESA, new courses including podcasting, sign language ('Flying Fingers'), and an art course for first and second graders, and the Fuel for the Weekend food program serving 127 families. Board members praised the program and asked about challenges and staff retention; Rayther said returning staff significantly outnumbered new staff this summer.

discussions.body: Alder Larson questioned where the $50,000 would come from (answer: reserves) and pressed for clarity on where future construction funds — potentially $20 million or more — would originate before spending on a feasibility study. Fire Chief Barnes explained that the study allocates $25,000 to FGMA Architects for the police side, $15,000 to Five Bugles for the fire side, and a reserve for potential environmental studies; she also outlined potential funding sources including $2 million allocated to the county from the UW system, congressionally directed spending, and state Department of Administration funds. Alder Kilian confirmed the plan would keep the fire department on the current footprint at Central Fire while expanding into the police department space, with 800 Grand Avenue potentially vacated. Alder Henke changed his position from committee (where he voted no) to support, citing newly learned funding opportunities. The motion by Trueblood, seconded by Tierney, failed to reach the required 2/3 majority; after the vote, Kilian raised the possibility of reconsideration at the September 8th meeting, and Chief Barnes asked whether returning with an amended funding structure that reduces the reserve draw could come back through committee.

title: City Council Meeting Pt.2
overview: The Wausau City Council reconvened from closed session to consider two major items: approving submission of an RFP response to Marathon County for the former UWSP Wausau campus at 518 South 17th Avenue, and approving an alternate bid for construction of up to 153 parking stalls in Riverfront Parking Lot E. Both items passed 6-2 and 6-1 (with one abstention) respectively, with the campus proposal representing a potential major relocation of the Wausau Police Department and other city functions, while the parking lot project fulfills obligations under a developers agreement related to Athletic Park.

discussions.item: RFP Response for Former UWSP Wausau Campus
discussions.body: City Director Randy Fyfe outlined the proposal, which includes relocating Wausau PD headquarters to the main campus building (potentially partnering with the Wausau School District), exploring public safety or recreation use for the field house, demolishing dormitories for new housing, converting the current police department building to a fire station, and identifying 815 Floral Avenue as a redevelopment opportunity. The purchase price offered is $1, with a requested 6-month due diligence period. Alder Larson expressed skepticism, citing past city land purchases that yielded no results and questioning the cost of maintaining a 66-year-old building versus DPW facility needs. Alder Watson, who serves on both the city council and county board, recused herself from active debate but voiced support. Alder Kilian raised concerns about including the Floral Avenue property in the RFP, and Fyfe indicated it could be removed at council's discretion. Alderwoman Trueblood emphasized the vote only commits the city to submitting the proposal, not to any final decision, and there is no cost to submit.

discussions.body: Alderwoman Trueblood moved to call the question on the UWSP campus RFP vote; an unnamed alderperson objected, triggering a procedural debate over council rules on terminating debate. After consultation with council rules, the objection was ultimately withdrawn, allowing the vote to proceed without a separate vote to call the question. A separate motion to suspend the rules related to item 6 (reconsideration of referral of resolution 26-0811) passed 6-2, with the presiding officer confirming that 6-2 constitutes the required two-thirds majority of members present.

discussions.item: Resolution 26-0811: Riverfront Parking Lot E Alternate Bid (PGA Inc.)
discussions.body: Director Lindman explained that the city is obligated under a developers agreement to provide approximately 150 new parking spaces near Athletic Park by May 2027. A city attorney opinion concluded the legal obligation was closer to 118 stalls given prior lot construction, but the developer Mark McDonald anticipated 153. The Board of Public Works awarded the base bid to PGA Inc. and referred the alternate bid (adding stalls up to 153) to the council. The base bid came in at $500,000 and the alternate bid added $57,500, totaling under the $650,000 budget. Alder Henning called it a 'no-brainer' given the savings. Alder Witkowski raised concerns about year-round utilization of the large lot, garbage issues near Athletic Park, and parking enforcement during ball games. Alder Tierney stated she would not support the alternate bid above 120 stalls, calling the extra stalls a want rather than a need. The motion passed 6-2.

title: Administrative Policy Committee Meeting
overview: The Village of Kronenwetter's Administrative Policy Committee met on August 18, 2026, with Finance Director John leading the majority of discussions focused on the upcoming property reassessment, 2026 equalized valuation data, existing debt obligations, and the newly drafted 2027-2036 Capital Improvement Program. The meeting was significant for residents as officials revealed the village is approximately 40% below required full market value assessment, that TID 1 faces serious financial pressure if the anticipated distribution center development does not proceed this fall, and that opportunities exist in 2029-2030 for strategic debt-financed infrastructure investment.

discussions.item: Approval of Minutes - June 15th Meeting
discussions.body: Trustee Mary Solheim moved to approve the June 15th meeting minutes as presented, seconded by Misty Swanson. The motion passed 4-0 with no discussion.

discussions.item: Property Reassessment Update
discussions.body: Finance Director John reported that the exterior reassessment will begin the week of August 24th, with five assessors working in the field. He explained the village is approximately 40% below required full market value and faces a state takeover of the reassessment — at two to three times the cost — if not completed by end of 2027. The reassessment is being funded through budget surpluses from prior years when positions were unfilled, avoiding any new budget line item. Trustee Guy Fridale raised concerns about negative social media commentary and suggested early, repeated public messaging that the village only controls its portion of the tax levy. John noted that no valuation changes will appear on the December 2026 tax bill and that some property owners seeing a below-average valuation increase could actually see a tax reduction. The committee also discussed reviewing potentially tax-exempt parcels that may no longer qualify.

discussions.item: 2026 Preliminary Equalized Valuation and TID Increments
discussions.body: John reported that the village's equalized valuation rose by approximately $101 million in 2026, nearly a 10% increase, now exceeding $1.2 billion, but that assessed valuation remains around $700 million — only about 63% of full market value. Net new construction came in at just 0.65% for the third consecutive year, limiting the village's allowable tax levy increase without an exception to approximately $12,000. TID 1 was identified as the village's most significant financial concern: a 12% drop in valuation from $21 million to $19 million resulted from assessor adjustments on two parcels near Kowalski and Highway 39, compounded by a state-issued prior year correction of $1.4 million. John emphasized that if the anticipated distribution center in TID 1 does not break ground this fall, the village could face a shortfall of $1.5 million or more by 2044, potentially depleting the general fund reserve built over recent years. Fridale observed that TIDs 2 and 4 are performing well and noted TID 3 closed in February.

discussions.item: July 2026 Budget Status Report
discussions.body: John reported that after seven months (58% of the year), the general fund had collected approximately 62% of budgeted revenues and spent about 49% of budgeted expenditures, indicating a healthy position. He cautioned that public works billing typically lags field work and that costs will increase. Three ongoing budget concerns — village attorney fees, municipal building costs, and garbage — remain unresolved. John acknowledged the 2025 audit has not yet been completed due to competing priorities including the reassessment launch and 2027 budget preparation, but expressed confidence that the audit could be finalized in time for the October budget workshops. Committee members praised John's work stabilizing village finances and noted the village operates with limited finance staff.

discussions.item: Review of Existing Debt Obligations Outstanding
discussions.body: John reviewed all outstanding debt, totaling approximately $14.5 million, of which $10 million is general obligation debt — representing only 17% of the village's $59 million maximum borrowing capacity. He identified the 2016 TID 1 redevelopment lease revenue bonds as a wait-and-see situation given low interest rates of 2.45-3.2% and the pending distribution center development. The 2024 general obligation bonds at 4-5% interest were flagged as a future refinancing candidate once callable in April 2029. He highlighted that debt service tax levy obligations drop significantly in 2029 (by ~$226,000) and 2030 (by ~$165,000), creating an opportunity window for infrastructure investment. Fridale and others emphasized the importance of TID 2 and TID 4 closure timelines — estimated around 2032 and 2033 respectively — as additional fiscal opportunities.

discussions.item: 2027-2036 Capital Improvement Program Budget
discussions.body: John and Public Works Director Greg presented the village's first-ever 10-year Capital Improvement Program, drafted using dedicated CIP software rather than Excel to improve accuracy and fluidity. The draft CIP covers projects across fire, municipal center, parks, police, public works, sewer, and water utilities, with a preliminary 2027 total of approximately $4.3 million. Funding sources include approximately $1.2 million in unused TID 2 bond proceeds that must be redirected if not spent on a TID project by October 2027, potential borrowing, utility depreciation funds, and donations. John noted the parks committee provided additional input the prior evening and that figures will be updated before the September presentation. The committee discussed potential borrowing scenarios — ranging from $1 million to $10 million — and agreed that a formal affordability analysis presenting multiple options would be prepared for the September APC meeting and budget workshops. No final decisions were made.

discussions.item: Rent Abatement Hearing - 615 Elm Street
discussions.body: Tenant Heather Fletcher testified she has lived at 615 Elm Street since June 2024, pays $990/month, and withheld approximately five months of rent (April through August) due to persistent basement flooding with standing water present since move-in, a leaking and improperly caulked shower, mold in the shower, improperly repaired windows (one clamped shut, constituting a fire hazard), and dehumidifiers running off her electricity plugged into a power strip sitting in standing water. Property manager Paul Dykstra and owner Mark Johnson of Better Tomorrow Investments testified they were not notified of water issues until May 4, 2026, when city violation notices arrived; they disputed the timeline and attributed basement water partly to the tenant's improperly installed air conditioning unit. overview: The Village of Weston Finance and HR Committee held its August meeting covering IT department budget review, July financial reports, TIF district updates, and 2027 budget priorities including potential new staff positions and robotic lawnmowers. The committee approved a contract for a final TIF One audit with Hawkins for $5,210 and voted to move forward with a pay grade reclassification recommendation following a closed session. A $4 million local bank loan for the Mountain Bay Police Headquarters was also announced as forthcoming to the full board.

discussions.item: Public Comment
discussions.body: One public commenter, identified as Jim from Council 53, raised concerns about the lack of staff time quantification in budget reports, specifically calling out the IT department's in-house application development and the pool budget as examples of incomplete financial data. He argued that decisions should be data-driven, noting that the pool budget failed to account for tourism funding, general fund contributions, concession revenues, and staff hours. He also expressed concern that the 2027 budget wish list lacked cost detail and called for a more analytical approach to financial decision-making across the village.

discussions.item: Approval of Minutes
discussions.body: A motion was made and seconded to approve the minutes from the previous Finance and HR meeting. The motion carried with no noted opposition.

discussions.item: July Budget Status Report and TIF Reports
discussions.body: Finance staff (referred to as Jessica) explained a significant revenue difference in the water utility fund between 2025 and 2026, attributing it to additional PASS money received in the prior year. On TIF One, Jessica noted that large disbursements reflected grant payouts to Tommy Docks and Oak River under developers' agreements, accelerated because TIF One is closing. Discussion arose about Wandering Springs West properties still held by the original developer (Gold Key Investments) that were supposed to be conveyed to the village; the committee discussed the ongoing legal effort to obtain quitclaim deeds, with Trustee Brent Olson providing historical context. Items 5, 6, and 7 were acknowledged together and the motion carried.

discussions.item: IT Department Budget Presentation
discussions.body: Technology Services Director Nate Crow presented a detailed overview of his department, noting it is a department of one covering GIS, network, servers, software, and phones. The 2026 operating budget is $141,745, with water and sewer utilities funding approximately 45-46% of his position. Total all-funds cost is approximately $361,000, with the general fund covering 62%. Crow highlighted cybersecurity risks to public water systems from a coordinated national attack originating in Minnesota, and explained $14,000 in outside services budget as a rapid-response cushion. Public Works staff endorsed the in-house Diggers Hotline mapping app, noting it eliminated the need for additional utility staff. Committee members asked about succession planning if Crow were unavailable; he noted Heartland Business Systems is on call for major incidents.

discussions.item: 2027 Budget Priorities
discussions.body: Finance Director Jessica and another staff member (Jamie) presented a priorities list for discussion. The committee discussed several items including: SAFER grant staffing positions (described as effectively already decided given public support), a new facilities and grounds maintenance position (committee requested a draft job description and discussion of utility cost-sharing, estimated at possibly 50/50 with utilities), robotic lawnmowers (committee expressed interest in starting with one unit to pilot at the safety building rather than two, noting concerns about cut quality), and the contracted mowing service of approximately $25,000/year that could partially offset a new position. The committee agreed to have staff price out all items on the list for upcoming joint budget meetings starting the week of August 24. The TIF One fund balance was discussed as a potential one-time capital funding source following required distribution to taxing jurisdictions.

discussions.item: Contract for Final Audit of TIF One
discussions.body: Jessica presented a proposal to engage Hawkins auditors for the required final TIF One audit at a quoted price of $5,210, noting they have previously performed TIF audits for the village and have consistently offered competitive pricing. The motion to approve was made and seconded, and carried unanimously with no discussion opposing the selection.

discussions.item: Employee Appreciation and Standing Monthly Staff Recognition
discussions.body: The committee discussed options for staff recognition, with public works director Michael cautioning that formal recognition programs have previously caused friction among staff who felt their contributions went unnoticed relative to those recognized. Several committee members suggested a standing monthly agenda item for department heads to voluntarily recognize staff accomplishments. The committee decided to table formal action and directed staff to raise the topic at the next all-staff meeting to gather employee input on what recognition approaches they would find meaningful.

discussions.item: Ethics Function Discussion
discussions.body: The committee chair introduced the concept of establishing a formal ethics function for the village, noting the board of trustees had referred the topic to this committee. An 11-page ethics ordinance from a neighboring municipality (Wausau) was shared as a reference. Given the presence of new committee members, no substantive action was taken; members were asked to review the materials and return with feedback next month. The chair noted the current village ethics policy routes complaints to department heads and does not address elected officials.

discussions.body: The committee moved into closed session under Wisconsin Statute 19.85(1)(c) to consider pay grade reclassifications for the utility clerk and fleet positions. Upon returning to open session, a motion was made and seconded to approve the reclassification recommendation, and it carried with no noted opposition.

discussions.body: Jessica announced that following the village board's approval of the Mountain Bay Police Headquarters design and bid, the finance department solicited quotes from local banks for a $4 million loan to accelerate funding, as going to market would take several months. She reported the local bank responses were very competitive and said the board would be asked to approve the loan at the next meeting.

discussions.body: Dan moved to approve the previous meeting minutes as presented; Patty seconded. No discussion followed. The motion passed unanimously on a voice vote.

discussions.item: Village Communications About Parks Within the Community
discussions.body: The committee reviewed the village website's park content, noting Jennifer had added videos in 2023 that were well-received. Members suggested promoting park videos on social media, adding short trail-walking videos, and including a notice in the village newsletter directing residents to check out park resources. Greg noted that once the Chromter Drive project wraps up, the village plans to add wayfinding signs near apartments directing people to trails at the municipal center.

discussions.item: 2026–2036 Capital Improvements Program Budget
discussions.body: The committee conducted a card-sorting exercise where each member wrote capital improvement ideas on cards, which were then grouped by park to identify priorities. The top vote-getter was the Bushka Park playground replacement (five or more cards), followed by Friendship/Cercas Park rubber surfacing replacement (estimated $70,000–$80,000), Towering Pines Park shelter and restroom development (proposed as a multi-year civic-style park project), and the municipal center park (restroom and potential disc golf course, estimated $150,000+). The committee tentatively assigned Bushka Park playground for 2027, Friendship Park surfacing for 2029, Towering Pines for 2030–2032, and municipal center park for 2033. General park signage, ADA improvements, and branding were discussed as ongoing priorities, with 2030 floated as an 'ADA year.' Civil Park new playground was placed at the end of the plan, approximately 2036–2037. Greg noted approximately $20,000 remains in a parks fund that could be directed toward near-term improvements such as a trail connecting Friendship Park to the dog park.

discussions.item: September 12, 2026 Bushka Park 5K Run/Walk Fundraiser
discussions.body: Erin Mishka reported $1,000 in sponsorships secured with a goal of $1,225 to fund participant shirts; no registration fee is charged and donations are voluntary. Chief [Cherry McHugh] approved a list of priority intersections for volunteer safety coverage, and committee members offered to staff intersections wearing high-visibility vests. The route was adjusted from the original plan so both the 3K and 5K now start and end at Bushka Park. Relocation (a local business) is hosting a raffle and 50/50 drawing, with the 50/50 beginning the week prior. Water stations will be set up at Bushka Park and civil park (halfway point), with Jennifer volunteering to cover water costs. Start time is 10 a.m. on a Saturday.

discussions.item: Future Fundraising Ideas — Living River Concert
discussions.body: Erin Mishka announced plans for a Living River Concert in May, with $1,000 in sponsorship already secured and an anonymous donor covering the band cost, resulting in no cost to the village. She proposed holding the event at Towering Pines and directing proceeds to the Bushka Park Fund Reserve. A committee member (Tim) raised a constituent concern about why residents must fundraise for parks rather than relying on tax dollars; other members acknowledged the concern but noted the village board has been supportive, including a $5,000 match on a recent grant. A running total of approximately $16,000 raised for Bushka Park was referenced.

discussions.item: Quick Fixes and Small Improvements
discussions.body: Members identified several non-capital quick fixes for parks crew attention: removing no-dog signs, repairing a broken plexiglass circle on old wooden playground equipment at Bushka, adding paper towel holders in restrooms, installing at least one handicap swing, adding a bike rack on the farmers market side of Bushka Park, refreshing old wooden park signs at Nor-a-Plaza, Friendship, and Gooding parks, adding sand and a net to the Savil Park volleyball court, and investigating bike route signage connectivity with Rothschild. Greg noted the parks crew has been pressure-washing slides, shelters, and equipment during the slow grass-cutting period.

discussions.item: Next Meeting Date
discussions.body: The committee discussed transitioning from bi-weekly to monthly or as-needed meetings, noting that Dan's return to teaching makes the 4 p.m. time slot difficult. After discussion, the group tentatively agreed to meet Tuesday, September 8 (pending confirmation that a quorum can attend), at 4:30 p.m., with the primary focus of reviewing CIP dollar amounts to present to the village board and finalizing 5K run details.
