discussions.item: Public Comment
discussions.body: Six residents spoke during public comment. Jim Pensol encouraged civic engagement and described how public turnout once reversed a board decision to rename Schofield Avenue to DC Everest Boulevard. Kyra Lenzo addressed the animal fancier licensing issue, defending her care of four huskies and offering to expand her fenced outdoor space to comply with any space requirements. A neighbor, identified as a Borcart family member at 604 North Lane, complained about waste runoff from Lenzo's dogs onto their property citing ordinance sections 10.12, 10.19, and 10.29. Scott Borcart (County Road H) and Tony Hase (Danny's Girls vendor) both urged the board to keep the farmers market at Kennedy Park, with Hase noting business had improved significantly since the Alderson roundabout opened. Steve Mel spoke on the rezoning item (agenda item 43), arguing the planning commission's denial was improperly influenced by planner Jennifer Higgins's personal preference against storage facilities and citing Wisconsin Act 67's limitations on CUP denials.

discussions.item: Joint Resolution 2026-0001: Mountain Bay Metro PD Headquarters Debt Authorization
discussions.body: Trustee Ermeling raised significant concerns about the repayment structure, noting that at $130,000 per year minimum, it could take approximately 34-40 years for Mountain Bay Metro PD to fully repay the municipalities for the construction loan, while Weston would need to increase its levy by roughly $206,000 annually to service the 20-year debt. Village Administrator and police representatives clarified that $130,000 is a minimum and that the Oversight Board can direct additional fund balance payments to accelerate repayment, with a goal of $250,000-$275,000 annually total from both municipalities. Ermeling and another trustee (believed to be Kern) voted no; the resolution passed 3-2. The agreement had been reviewed by Rothschild's financial advisors and Mountain Bay Metro's attorney but not Weston's own attorney, which Ermeling flagged as a concern for a multi-million-dollar commitment.

discussions.item: Farmers Market Location at Kennedy Park
discussions.body: The board voted 4-1 to continue the farmers market at Kennedy Park, with Trustee Ermeling casting the lone dissenting vote, expressing concern that the park's green space was being consumed. Trustee Olson outlined several proposed mitigation measures including enhanced parking enforcement, coning off intersections 15 feet in each direction, and reaching out to a neighboring property owner about sight-obscuring vegetation. Trustee Lopes-Serrao argued the market pays for itself, serves as a community gathering event, and that no viable alternative location exists. Village President Maloney said he has visited the market at least ten times and found it a positive experience. A suggestion to survey vendors and customers again after the Alderson roundabout opened was raised by Ermeling and supported by others as a future step.

discussions.item: Municipal Center Rooms as Public Meeting/Gathering Spaces
discussions.body: The board discussed but took no action on a proposal to open municipal center meeting rooms to the public for gatherings, a topic raised at a prior community engagement session. Multiple trustees and staff expressed opposition based on past experience with damage, cleaning costs, and supervision burdens — Clerk Pam described specific problems from her time at Schofield Township, including vandalism and post-party cleanup that exceeded security deposits. Trustee Olson said he was not firmly opposed but would not support it without an alternative to requiring staff supervision on weekends. No action was taken.

discussions.item: Rezoning Request: 4205 & 4307 Weston Avenue (B2 to LI) — Storage Facility
discussions.body: Trustee Lopes-Serrao moved to accept the Planning Commission's recommendation of denial for the rezoning of 4205 and 4307 Weston Avenue from B2 Highway Business to LI Limited Industrial for a proposed personal storage unit facility. A procedural issue was raised: overturning the planning commission's denial requires a 2/3 supermajority (five of seven votes), but with only five trustees present, all five would need to vote in favor of rezoning — effectively requiring unanimity to override. The motion to accept the denial received a second, and the transcript ends before the vote is recorded.

discussions.item: 2027 Budget Priorities
discussions.body: The Finance and HR Committee brought three preliminary priorities to the full board: one robotic mower pilot, a new facilities and grounds maintenance position, and three SAFER grant-funded fire/EMS staff positions phased in over 2027. Trustees discussed broadening the scope to include public safety (EMS, fire, police), drinking water infrastructure, code enforcement, and cybersecurity. Trustee Beck emphasized multi-year budget planning similar to the CIP process used in public works. A recent village comprehensive plan survey was cited showing road maintenance and EMS tied as top community priorities. No formal action was taken; further discussion is scheduled for a budget session on the 24th at 5:30.

title: Executive Committee Meeting
overview: The Marathon County Executive Committee held a lengthy meeting focused on the Hub City Wind project in southwestern Marathon County, featuring public comment from 10 residents, a panel discussion with legal experts and municipal officials, and concluding with a motion to forward the question of whether to pursue a Joint Development Agreement (JDA) to the full 38-member county board. The committee heard from attorneys, a UW-Extension local government educator, and a town chair from Wood County about the limited legal authority counties have over large-scale wind projects under Wisconsin statute, with experts uniformly concluding that a JDA is effectively the strongest tool available to the county.

discussions.item: Public Comment – Hub City Wind Project
discussions.body: Ten speakers addressed the committee on the Hub City Wind project. Speakers were divided: several opposed the project citing concerns about tourism impacts on Rib Mountain viewsheds, farmland destruction, health effects, wildlife harm, road damage, and skepticism about JDA benefits, with Joe Bergen urging the county to control any JDA drafting and Nikki Catrell calling for a moratorium and intervenor status. Supporters Dan Bar and Kathy Conley Bar argued for renewable energy as a climate response. Wendy Rogolski specifically demanded that any decision to pursue JDA negotiations be made in open session with a recorded vote, not behind closed doors. James Yeetus urged the county to fight the project through litigation or ordinance rather than negotiate.

discussions.item: Staff Presentation: PSC Intervention Process and County Research Memos
discussions.body: CPZ Director Lori Kimmons presented two memos. The first summarized conversations with PSC staff about the intervention process, noting counties have a 14-day window to apply for intervenor status after a notice of proceeding, that the PSC staff could not recall any project ever being fully denied through intervention, and that intervention is costly and time-consuming. The second memo summarized conversations with staff and officials in Columbia, Iowa, Kenosha, St. Croix counties and the Town of Saratoga in Wood County, all of whom reported using JDAs as their primary tool and recommended early negotiation over PSC intervention. Staff's overall recommendation was to begin engaging the developer as soon as possible about a potential JDA.

discussions.item: Panel: Town of Saratoga Experience with JDA
discussions.body: Laura Fure, Town Chair and Zoning Administrator for the Town of Saratoga in Wood County, described her community's experience with a 150-megawatt solar project owned outright by the developer (not leased). The town hired an independent Madison law firm paid for by the developer to draft the JDA, required a decommissioning plan, and receives approximately $350,000 per year in shared revenues (county receives about two-thirds). She said the biggest surprises were the size and danger of battery storage systems, enlarged transmission line easements, and that these unknowns are now being addressed in a second solar JDA currently underway. She stated the town felt it had significant control through the JDA process.

discussions.item: Panel: Legal Authority and JDA Framework – Andy Phillips (Atollis Law) and Bill Oman (UW Extension)
discussions.body: Attorney Andy Phillips explained that under Wisconsin statute 66.0401(1m), counties can regulate renewable energy projects on a case-by-case basis but that statute 196.491 preempts local regulation for projects 100 megawatts or more once the PSC issues a CPCN, meaning the county has no authority to stop such a project through ordinance. He said JDAs are the most effective tool counties have to address decommissioning, road damage, setbacks, and emergency response. Bill Oman of UW-Extension agreed entirely, noting the legislature deliberately preempted local authority to promote renewable energy, that legislative efforts to restore local control failed in the most recent session, and that updating a comprehensive plan is the only other tool available but that the PSC has never denied a project based on inconsistency with a local comp plan. Both strongly recommended JDAs as the primary protective mechanism.

discussions.item: Executive Committee Q&A with Panelists
discussions.body: Supervisors asked wide-ranging questions. On moratoriums, Phillips said a short-duration moratorium (6–18 months) aimed at developing new regulations is legally defensible but one designed simply to block a project would likely be struck down; Oman agreed. On intervention, Phillips noted his firm has filed appeals in two cases where JDA negotiations broke down after a CPCN was issued. On road damage, Phillips recommended addressing repairs proactively in a JDA rather than relying on retrospective treble-damage statutes (86.02 and 86.14). On decommissioning, Phillips said JDAs should require financial assurance such as bonds, especially because developers often sell projects to regulated utilities. On attorney fees, Phillips confirmed that in executed JDAs the developer has always paid county attorney fees, though fee caps are currently being contested in pending negotiations. Supervisor Hau asked about health damage compensation and energy going off the local grid; Phillips said neither falls within county authority and landowner health concerns should be addressed between landowners and the developer directly. Supervisor Dickinson questioned why a developer with no legal obligation to sign a JDA would do so, with Phillips responding that a signed JDA allows the developer to check off PSC decision-matrix issue number three — compliance with orderly land use — but that the other 10 PSC decision criteria still must be addressed independently.

discussions.item: Motion to Forward JDA Discussion to Full County Board
discussions.body: Vice Chair Boots moved to forward to the full county board a recommendation to discuss whether to pursue a potential JDA, stating the full 38-member board should have input on a decision of this magnitude. Supervisor Morash seconded. Debate followed, with Supervisor Griner expressing concern that the committee had focused almost entirely on JDA options without adequately exploring other tools listed in the packet. Supervisor Morash said a moratorium was not a viable option given the existing ordinance and that all PSC-reviewed projects have been approved regardless of intervention. Supervisor Robinson agreed the sequence of decisions mattered — noting that pursuing a JDA does not guarantee Alliance will come to the table. Supervisor Dickinson noted the committee had not discussed the comprehensive plan amendment option in depth. Chair Gibbs clarified the motion: the board would discuss whether to pursue JDA negotiations, and any resulting agreement would still require future action. The motion carried, though the tally was not stated.

publicComment: Ten speakers signed up and were given 3 minutes each. Joe Bergen (Town of Day) urged the county to control any JDA drafting and protect the Rib Mountain viewshed. Dan Bar (Town of Nolton) spoke in favor of renewable energy and entering a strong JDA. Kathy Conley Bar expressed support for climate action while acknowledging community concerns. Mary Clus (Wausau) argued that not pursuing a JDA would be fiscally irresponsible and spoke on behalf of Wisconsin Farmers Union's Marathon County chapter opposing giving away county power. Cindy Nielsen (Town of O'Plane) strongly opposed the project, citing impacts on farming, animal health, and road infrastructure, and warned supervisors of electoral consequences. Mark Radkey (Town of O'Plane) noted that the alternative energy advisory committee survey and public forums showed overwhelming opposition to a JDA. James Yeetus (Town of Easton) urged the county to fight the project through ordinances and litigation rather than negotiate. Dean Beck (Town of Easton) raised concerns about turbine efficiency loss from bug residue, requested utility payments be based on actual rather than projected production, and suggested revenues be held in escrow for impacted non-participating landowners. Wendy Rogolski (Town of Green Valley, appearing online) demanded that any decision to authorize JDA negotiations be made openly with a recorded public vote, not in closed session. Nikki Catrell (Town of Brighton) called for a moratorium, urged the county to apply for intervenor status, requested independent third-party analysis of Alliant's submissions, and presented an evidence matrix of 30 potential challenges tied to Wisconsin CPCN requirements.

title: Infrastructure and Facilities Committee Meeting
overview: The Wausau Infrastructure and Facilities Committee met on August 13th and approved multiple action items including parking restriction corrections, utility easements, DOT transportation agreements for Grand Avenue and Business 51 reconstruction, a mowing ordinance amendment, a stormwater maintenance agreement, a bicycle sidewalk ordinance change, retired city sign disposition, and a bollard encroachment permit. The committee rejected both a Lamar billboard easement and a rectangular rapid flashing beacon at Thomas Street and River Drive, and held a significant discussion about the potential purchase of county highway property at 1430, 1308, and 1212 West Street for a new fleet maintenance facility potentially shared with Metro Ride.

discussions.item: A: Parking Restrictions on Greenfield Avenue from Fernwood Drive to Summit Drive
discussions.body: Staff described this as a housekeeping item: a November 1st to April 1st seasonal restriction tied to snow plowing had been approved at committee but was omitted when the item went to the full council. The amendment was moved, seconded, and approved unanimously with no notable debate.

discussions.item: B: Easement with Wisconsin Public Service at 1603 Martin Street
discussions.body: Staff explained this utility easement allows Wisconsin Public Service to run electricity across a city-owned parcel to reach a wastewater lift station under construction. The item was approved without discussion.

discussions.item: C: Easement for Win LLC at 814 North 1st Street
discussions.body: Staff described this as another housekeeping correction: the easement had previously been approved but was incorrectly labeled as going to Alexco rather than Win LLC, preventing council approval. The corrected easement was moved and approved unanimously.

discussions.item: D-G: Business 51/Grand Avenue DOT Transportation Agreements
discussions.body: Staff walked through four related items: a transportation project plat for Grand Avenue (Lake View Drive to Kent Street) where DOT reimburses the city 100% for right-of-way acquisition; a revised state-municipal finance agreement for the same project with the city responsible for approximately $595,000 in utility costs and 25% of design; a financing agreement for Business 51 from County Trunk Highway U to West Campus Drive with the city responsible for only $5,340 in utility adjustments; and a maintenance agreement for the same Business 51 corridor committing the city to maintain crosswalks, ped ramps, and plow intersections. A committee member asked whether additional revisions to the Grand Avenue agreement were anticipated before 2029; staff said no given the 60% plan stage. Another member noted increased maintenance responsibilities for new ped ramps and crosswalks. All four items were approved.

discussions.item: H: Amending Section 6.48.010 Mowing Requirement
discussions.body: A committee member raised concerns that the existing ordinance language was confusing—residents were receiving citations for boulevard mowing but the obligation was not clearly codified, and language about prohibited plantings could be interpreted to allow certain gardens. Staff confirmed enforcement had generally been complaint-driven and that the ordinance was intended to mirror lawn maintenance expectations. One member moved to approve as written, arguing the intent was clear; another requested a future agenda item to address broader boulevard use communication and potential pollinator garden policy. The mowing requirement amendment was approved, and a future agenda item on boulevard ordinance communication was requested.

discussions.item: I: Stormwater Maintenance Agreement with Beacon Resources LLC at 731 North First Street
discussions.body: Staff described this as a routine maintenance agreement required for any property redeveloped over one acre to ensure stormwater facilities are maintained. A member asked about verification mechanisms; staff confirmed periodic inspections occur. The item was approved without significant debate.

discussions.item: J: Amending Section 10.40.040 - Bicycling on Sidewalk near Thomas Street Bridge
discussions.body: Staff, presenting on behalf of the Bicycle and Pedestrian Advisory Committee, explained the amendment would legalize bicycling on the sidewalk along a short gap between Thomas Street Bridge and Oak Island Park on River Edge Parkway, with the long-term intent of building a multi-use path to close the infrastructure gap. One member raised safety concerns about cyclists encountering pedestrians on the curved, hilly sidewalk; staff noted bike-ped committee discussed this and found on-street risk greater, and that use of the sidewalk would be optional ('may' language). The item had already passed Public Health and Safety Committee. It was approved.

discussions.item: K: Sign Disposition Plan for Retired City Signs
discussions.body: Staff reported four city signs were replaced, two retained, and that there is significant interest from both private buyers and the Marathon County Historical Society. The plan called for giving one sign to the historical society and selling the other per municipal code. A committee member moved to amend the motion so the Marathon County Historical Society could choose which sign they preferred rather than staff selecting for them. That amended motion was approved unanimously.

discussions.item: L: Rectangular Rapid Flashing Beacon at Thomas Street and River Drive
discussions.body: Staff noted that engineering did not recommend approval because pedestrian count thresholds were not met, though the Bicycle and Pedestrian Advisory Committee had forwarded the item citing future development at 700 Grand and proximity to the River Edge Parkway system. One member said placing a beacon 500 feet from the recently approved Thomas and McCleary beacon did not make sense from a traffic standpoint and noted the county is soliciting redevelopment proposals for nearby property. Another member argued the committee should follow its own standards or render them meaningless. A motion to table until after completion of 700 Grand was withdrawn after a member argued denial was cleaner. A motion to approve was then made and seconded; the motion failed with multiple nay votes.

discussions.item: M: Non-Binding Letter of Intent with TLC Properties/Lamar for Billboard Easement at 1514 North 3rd Street
discussions.body: Staff explained Lamar sought a permanent easement for the billboard on Bridge Street on city-owned property, but staff recommended against it to preserve future redevelopment flexibility. A member noted the city renewed Lamar's lease in short terms specifically to maintain that flexibility and characterized a permanent easement as a great deal for Lamar but not the city. Multiple members opposed granting a permanent easement. A motion to approve was made for procedural purposes; the motion failed on a nay vote.

discussions.item: O: Encroachment Permit for 630 North 3rd Street
discussions.body: Staff explained that the property owner, Randy Williams, wants to install bollards to protect stone copings on a recently rehabbed building from snow plow damage; because the building sits at the right-of-way line, the bollards would encroach into city right-of-way. Engineering had no objection. Members discussed aesthetic compatibility with other downtown bollards and confirmed the property owner is responsible for installation, maintenance, and removal. The encroachment permit was approved.

discussions.item: Discussion: County Highway Property at 1430, 1308, and 1212 West Street for Fleet Maintenance Facility
discussions.body: The DPW director reported that after approximately 18 months of conversations, the county administrator indicated openness to receiving a purchase offer for the roughly 12-acre property, which could house both a new city fleet maintenance facility and a Metro Ride transit facility, enabling shared wash stations, bulk fluid storage, and other infrastructure. Staff noted most or all existing county structures would need to be demolished and rebuilt. A member asked for valuations of the current DPW fleet facility and Metro Ride property to understand potential offsets. Staff noted up to three acres fronting 17th Street could potentially be sold for redevelopment. Members noted the property's proximity to the parks department and potentially the police department. No formal action could be taken as this was a discussion item; committee expressed general support for continuing negotiations.

title: Human Resources, Finance, & Property Committee
committee: Marathon County Human Resources, Finance, & Property Committee
overview: The Marathon County Human Resources, Finance & Property Committee met to address several significant items including a tattoo convention licensing fee restructure, 2027 budget development discussions, position reclassifications, and a resolution to proceed with Phase 3 construction planning for a new county highway facility. The committee approved a modified health department fee schedule for body art establishments, approved a slate of position changes and reclassifications for the 2027 budget, authorized Phase 3 highway facility planning, and approved July claims totaling approximately $13.7 million.

discussions.item: Public Comment — Tattoo Convention Licensing
discussions.body: Three speakers addressed the committee regarding agenda item 6B6. Dave Bruo, representing the Village of Rothschild as tourism marketing director, outlined the economic impact of the Cedar Creek Ink Fest tattoo convention, estimating approximately $497,000 in total economic impact and $1,500 in county tax revenue based on 3,000 attendees. Mark Hannenburg, owner of Marked Up Tattoos and holder of one of the 32 permanent body art establishment licenses in Marathon County, supported the fee restructure concept but raised concerns about fairness of mid-year fee changes affecting permanent establishments that already renewed. Brandy Cannenburgg, assisting the event organizers, noted that under the current interpretation, 46 to 60 separate licenses would be required at a cost of $9,568 to $18,480, and argued a single event-level license may be legally correct under existing statute, noting Sauk County licensed the same organizer's convention as a single establishment.

discussions.item: 6B6 — Health Department Fee Schedule Modification for Tattoo and Piercing Licenses
discussions.body: Administrator Leonard and Health Department Director Kate Floric explained the proposed change would restructure establishment licensing fees on a tiered, practitioner-based model — one license covering up to six practitioners — for both permanent and temporary establishments, replacing the current per-establishment interpretation. Floric noted the change would actually represent a slight decrease (to approximately $208) for existing permanent establishments and would result in an estimated net levy impact of negative $400 in a normal year. Vice Chair [inaudible] confirmed that the new fee structure would be cheaper for the Cedar Creek Ink Fest than the current interpretation. The committee voted to approve the modified fee schedule, which will proceed to the full county board.

discussions.item: 6A1 — 2027 Budget Development and Policy Recommendations
discussions.body: Administrator Leonard presented updates on budget development, noting departments are reviewing fees against a board-directed 3% increase benchmark. Preliminary data showed equalized valuation grew 6.25% and net new construction at 1.545%, yielding approximately $800,000 in new levy capacity. Supervisor [inaudible, likely Robinson] pressed on whether the county must spend the new levy capacity, and Administrator Leonard explained that given existing debt obligations and rising costs, not maximizing the operating levy would be fiscally unsound. Supervisor [inaudible] noted the tax rate has dropped from $6.87 per $1,000 in 2006 to approximately $3.45 due to levy limits outpacing equalized value growth, and Vice Chair P expressed preference for spending only on existing needs rather than new programs.

discussions.item: 6A2 — Position Requests and Reclassifications for 2027 Budget
discussions.body: Administrator Leonard presented a comprehensive list of position changes across multiple departments, including the DA's office (abolish one restitution specialist, create one victim witness specialist and 0.5 administrative specialist), Corrections (eliminate administrative position, create corrections officer), Clerk of Courts (reclass to administrative specialist), Medical Examiner (abolish vacant deputy chief physician position, create senior administrative specialist), Administration (reclass driven by tax foreclosure duties), Health Department (abolish lab tech, create sanitarian; restructure business manager to senior admin plus new finance accountant), Social Services (child support realignment and six new CLTS positions fully funded by Medicaid), and Facilities/Capital Management (abolish maintenance tech, create maintenance specialist). Supervisor Jang expressed hesitation about approving all positions at once without knowing which had already been vetted, and Administrator Leonard clarified that all items except the Facilities/Capital Management position and the Administration reclass (going to Executive the next day) had already been approved by standing committees, several unanimously. Vice Chair Boots, attending remotely via WebEx, confirmed Health and Human Services approved the relevant items 7-0. Chair Gibbs moved to approve the position changes for the 2027 budget planning process, contingent on executive committee approving the administration reclass.

discussions.item: July Claims and Question Costs
discussions.body: The committee considered July claims totaling approximately $13,685,665. No substantive discussion occurred beyond a quip about health insurance and asphalt costs. The motion to approve passed unanimously.

discussions.item: Claims Disallowance — Schillinger
discussions.body: Corporation Counsel explained the statutory claims process, noting the county's insurance company recommended disallowing the Schillinger claim. The committee voted to disallow the claim; notice will be sent by certified mail.

discussions.item: 6B1 — Resolution Authorizing Phase 3 Highway Facility Construction Planning
discussions.body: Facilities Director Chris [inaudible] summarized design progress, including completed zoning change in the Village of Kronenwetter, ongoing site plan approval, preliminary site clearing and home demolitions, and a planned September bidding process to generate a guaranteed maximum price (GMP). Administrator Leonard and Finance Director Sam [inaudible] presented two financing scenarios: issuing approximately $20.3 million in new general obligation debt (at current ~4% rates costing roughly $9.5 million in interest) versus using accumulated North Central Healthcare revenues by transitioning existing Lake View campus debt to the debt levy over time, potentially avoiding a new large bond issuance and saving an estimated $4 million in interest. The strategy would generate cumulative funds sufficient to cover a $20–25 million project gap by approximately 2030–2033 depending on equalized value growth. The resolution does not commit funding but authorizes continued design finalization and bidding, with a final project authorization presentation expected by the October 15 county board education meeting.

publicComment: Three speakers offered public comment, all related to the tattoo convention licensing fee item. Dave Bruo (167949 Luchwagger Drive, Ringle), representing the Village of Rothschild as tourism marketing director, presented an economic impact analysis projecting approximately $497,000 in total economic impact from the Cedar Creek Ink Fest tattoo convention. Mark Hannenburg, owner of Marked Up Tattoos in Marathon County, supported restructuring fees but asked that any changes to permanent establishment fees take effect at each business's next renewal rather than mid-year. Brandy Cannenburgg, assisting event organizers, described the current fee structure as potentially requiring 46–60 licenses costing up to $18,480 for a three-day event, and noted the matter remains legally unresolved in her view, while prioritizing a clear licensing structure before the October 16–18 event.

title: Presentation
overview: The Wausau Common Council was unable to hold its regularly scheduled meeting due to a lack of quorum — fewer than the required eight members were present due to last-minute call-ins. Instead, the council held an informal presentation to honor Sheryl Bahr (referred to as 'Cheryl Barr' on her certificate) for 28 years of service on the Wausau Police and Fire Commission, from 1998 to 2026. No official council business was conducted and no votes were taken.

discussions.item: Quorum Failure
discussions.body: Mayor Diny opened by announcing that due to last-minute call-ins, the council did not have the required quorum of eight members and therefore the regular Common Council meeting would not be called to order. No official business was transacted.

discussions.item: Retirement Presentation for Sheryl Bahr
discussions.body: Mayor Diny provided historical context about Wausau in 1998 when Bahr joined the Police and Fire Commission. Police Chief Matt Barnes spoke, noting that every sworn member of the Wausau Police Department — including himself — had been interviewed by Bahr, and praised her ability to put candidates at ease. The fire chief also spoke, noting that Bahr had participated in interviews for nearly every member of the fire department as well as all promotions in both departments, emphasizing her attentiveness and follow-up questions. Bahr received a certificate of recognition and a plaque and offered brief remarks praising Wausau as 'one of the greatest cities in the United States' and lauding the integrity of the police and fire departments.

discussions.item: Certificate Presentation
discussions.body: Mayor Diny read aloud the certificate: 'City of Wausau, Wisconsin recognizes Cheryl Bar in recognition and appreciation of your leadership, insight, and dedication as a commissioner of the Wausau Police and Fire Commission from 1998 to 2026.' A plaque and a signed card from fire department members were also presented. The event concluded with applause and the informal meeting was adjourned.

title: Finance Committee Meeting
overview: The Wausau Finance Committee met on August 12, 2026 and approved five action items in a brief session, including hiring an insurance consultant to competitively bid the city's property and casualty coverage for the first time since 2007, two sole-source equipment purchases for Public Works and the Municipal Airport, and two bond issuances totaling nearly $6.8 million to fund the 2026 lead service line replacement program. The meeting was significant for residents as the bond financing at a 0.25% interest rate — with a forgivable portion — represents a favorable deal for both the water utility and property owners with private lateral replacements.

discussions.item: Approval of July 28, 2026 Finance Committee Minutes
discussions.body: A committee member moved to approve the minutes as recorded, with Henke providing the second. No discussion was held and the motion carried on a voice vote.

discussions.item: Gander Consulting Group — Insurance Consulting Services for 2027 Renewal
discussions.body: Finance staff (identified as Mary Ann) explained the city has been with SIVIC since 2007 without competitive review. She noted Gander Consulting would issue an RFP, review proposals, and recommend the best deal while accounting for ancillary services SIVIC provides, including NeoGov learning used by HR at no cost. The likely competitor would be the League policy. Staff recommended keeping MPIC for property insurance since the city switched to them only two years ago. A committee member noted '20 years is a long time to be with a single carrier.' The motion to authorize the engagement carried unanimously on a voice vote, moved by Neil and seconded by Henke.

discussions.item: Sole Source — Stacking Conveyor from Kafka Conveyors and Equipment Inc.
discussions.body: Solomon from Public Works confirmed the conveyor is at end of life, heavily corroded from years of stacking salt, and that Kafka holds the original design plans, making sole source appropriate and cost-effective. Finance director Mary Ann concurred with the sole source justification. Alder Neale raised the question of written justification to the finance director, which was addressed. The motion carried unanimously, moved by Neale and seconded by Henke.

discussions.item: Sole Source — Jet A Refueler from Wheels/Phillips 66 for Wausau Municipal Airport
discussions.body: Solomon explained the current refueler dates to 1996 and that purchasing this used unit conforms to Phillips 66 contract requirements with Wausau Flying Service and saves significant money over new procurement. He noted bids were obtained from Garsite, Westmore, and Skymark through Phillips 66 but all came in significantly higher. A committee member asked clarifying questions about the sole source justification and expressed satisfaction with the due diligence. The chair noted the prior arrangement involved the city reimbursing Wausau Flying Service and Phillips 66, making direct ownership cleaner. The motion carried unanimously, moved by Neale and seconded by [inaudible].

discussions.item: Water System Revenue Bond Series 2026 — Up to $3,469,102 (Lead Service Line — Utility Side)
discussions.body: Mary Ann explained this 0.25% fixed-rate Safe Drinking Water loan with a forgivable portion funds the utility side of the 2026 lead service line replacement program, with Five Star already performing work under a previously authorized contract. A committee member asked about the impact on water rates, and staff indicated Ehlers will return to the commission in September with a financial analysis; a rate case may be forthcoming. Total water utility debt was estimated at approximately $145 million as of December 31, 2025. Staff noted the loan is drawn down like a construction loan rather than paid out in a lump sum, with the DNR reviewing each draw for eligibility. The motion carried, moved by Henke and seconded by Neale.

discussions.item: General Obligation Promissory Notes Series 2026B — Up to $3,331,289 (Lead Service Line — Private Side)
discussions.body: This taxable GO note covers the private lateral replacement side of the same lead service line program at 0.25% interest, structured as a 10-year note resulting in approximately $340,000 in annual repayments. Staff confirmed the city expects to draw close to the full amount with some contingency. Mary Ann flagged that 2027 lead service line funding applications are already submitted and a similar financing gap will need to come before the committee. The motion carried, moved by Henke and seconded by Neale.

title: Water Works Commission Meeting
overview: The Wausau Water Works Commission held its August 12, 2026 meeting, covering a fluoride supply shortage that has prompted the utility to cut dosing to half normal levels, ongoing GAC carbon vessel change-outs for PFAS treatment, and a detailed corrosion control treatment study presentation from CDM Smith recommending addition of orthophosphate at 1 mg/L to reduce lead levels ahead of new federal regulations. The commission voted to approve a proposal for a PFAS process waste tank and chemical room addition project estimated at approximately $2.5 million, to be partially funded by $1.667 million in federal grant funds.

Item 1: Consideration and approval of minutes from July 14, 2026 meeting
Item 2: Director's report — fluoride supply shortage update

Item 3: Presentation by CDM Smith on Wausau Waterworks Corrosion Control Treatment Study

discussions.item: Approval of July 14, 2026 Meeting Minutes
discussions.body: The chair called for a motion to approve the minutes. A motion was made by Gellhar and seconded by Hadley. The minutes were approved by voice vote with no corrections noted.

discussions.item: Fluoride Supply Shortage
discussions.body: Staff identified as Scott reported that the utility received a fluoride shipment last month but was advised the next shipment may not arrive until late next month, prompting a reduction of fluoride dosing to approximately half the normal level, consistent with actions taken by larger communities facing the same shortage. Staff noted the DNR has approved the approach and that staff is attempting to reach the county health department director for guidance on whether to notify dental offices, schools, and other entities of the reduction. One commissioner noted the CDC has been working on fluoride elimination since April, to which the chair responded the commission had previously heard public debate on fluoride.

discussions.item: GAC Carbon Vessel Change-Out and PFAS Performance
discussions.body: Scott reported that the first GAC carbon change-out on August 5–6 went well, with Carbon Activated Corporation praised for professionalism, and that the next change-out is scheduled for September 3 using regenerated carbon from the first vessel. Staff noted that carbon saturation is occurring faster than anticipated — the vessels are not lasting the expected two years on regenerated carbon — and that change-outs will need to be expedited. Staff explained they are monitoring influent PFAS levels, which have remained stable, and are working to find the operational 'sweet spot' to maximize carbon longevity while staying under the 4 parts per trillion PFAS limit required by 2029. A commissioner asked whether influent PFAS concentrations are increasing; staff confirmed they are not.

discussions.item: CDM Smith Corrosion Control Treatment Study Presentation
discussions.body: CDM Smith representatives Amu Itasi and Javier Lockson presented findings from a roughly year-and-a-half pipe loop study required by the Wisconsin DNR due to Wausau's treatment process change. Key findings included: the new treatment plant did not significantly change lead mineral phases on pipe scale; fifth-liter sampling (required under the new Lead and Copper Rule Improvements effective 2028) showed a 90th percentile lead concentration of 19.2 micrograms per liter, exceeding both current and upcoming action levels, versus 14.2 for first-liter sampling which would have kept the system in compliance; and orthophosphate at 1 mg/L produced the best results, reducing lead concentrations and variability without the particulate lead release seen at 3 mg/L. The DNR accepted the study and directed Wausau to begin dosing orthophosphate at 1 mg/L with the system operational by July 2028, though CDM Smith recommended having it online by spring 2026 to allow 8–12 months for the treatment to take effect before new sampling requirements begin. Commissioners asked about health effects of orthophosphate (deemed safe and widely used since the 1990s), impacts on wastewater phosphorus loads (existing plant already designed to handle phosphorus removal), biological growth risks in the distribution system, and whether the existing sodium silicate corrosion control would continue alongside orthophosphate (confirmed yes, for now).

discussions.item: PFAS Process Waste Tank and Chemical Room Project Proposal
discussions.body: Director Eric explained that $1.667 million in federal grant funds originally earmarked for carbon change-outs can no longer be used for that purpose and must be applied to a capital project. The proposal calls for an underground process waste tank — needed because the existing 100,000-gallon tank causes plant operational lockouts during frequent carbon change-out backwashing — plus a chemical room addition for orthophosphate dosing and a storage room convertible to a future chemical room. The total project is estimated at approximately $2.5 million, leaving a projected shortfall of $700,000–$800,000 after the grant. Susan from Donahue Engineering confirmed the estimate. Staff noted a pending EPA verification on the competitive procurement process used to select Donahue. Commissioners were told an updated capital plan would be presented by Aylers on September 1st. Motion to approve was made by Hadley and seconded by Van Craig; the proposal was approved by voice vote.

title: Public Safety Committee Pt.1
overview: The Marathon County Public Safety Committee met on August 11, 2026 to discuss 2027 budget development, including nonprofit funding, sheriff's office fleet strategy, jail fees, new position requests, and ordinance updates. The committee approved forwarding several items to the county board, including new position reclassifications, an amendment to the chief deputy appointment ordinance, and creation of a non-lapsing contingency account for the medical examiner's office. A lengthy educational presentation on Flock Safety automated license plate reader (ALPR) technology was underway when the transcript ends.

discussions.item: Nonprofit Funding - Women's Community ($55,000)
discussions.body: Jane Graham Jennings, executive director of the Women's Community, presented on how the organization uses its $55,000 annual county contract, noting the funding covers approximately 16% of the $348,822 cost of contracted services and is used to leverage an additional $350,000 in state and federal grants. She highlighted services including lethality assessment protocol screening with the sheriff's department, domestic violence advocacy, sexual assault education in schools, and child advocacy center support. County Administrator Leonard indicated his plan is to keep nonprofit funding flat in the 2027 budget.

discussions.item: Sheriff's Office Fleet Strategy and Rolling Stock
discussions.body: Finance Director Chris (last name not clearly stated) presented a memo outlining a plan developed with Enterprise fleet services to address the gap in vehicle acquisitions caused by flat funding and failure to follow through on a CPI-based increase plan. The plan involves rolling existing leases, extending others with remaining mileage, and moving 17 vehicles into the lease fleet program, with a projected funding gap of $138,876 between existing rolling stock funds and the proposed $456,548 CIP allocation for 2027. Committee members discussed the bottleneck caused by upfitting vehicles at Belco in Columbus, and the sheriff described an effort to pursue a state innovation grant to create a regional upfitting operation involving Wausau, Mountain Bay, and Kronenwetter police departments. Administrator Leonard confirmed outreach to NTC, McDevco, and WATTA workforce organizations to support that effort. No resolution was presented, as fleet funding is not formally approved until November budget adoption.

discussions.item: Jail Stay Fees
discussions.body: Sheriff's Captain Chad (last name not clearly stated) presented a memo explaining that while the jail collected $303,666 in total fees in 2025, the portion attributable specifically to first-day fees ($30) and daily pay-for-stay fees ($20) is much smaller because roughly 90% of the jail population is pre-sentenced and not assessed those charges. Staff noted the population is largely indigent, making collections very difficult, and that even fee increases would not meaningfully increase actual revenue. Administrator Leonard noted a housekeeping amendment will be brought forward to update ordinance section 5.11 to reference the fee schedule rather than listing specific amounts, after an oversight was identified where the old fee remained in the ordinance text.

discussions.item: New Position Requests and Reclassifications for 2027 Budget
discussions.body: Administrator Leonard presented four personnel actions: (1) DA's office - abolish a county-funded restitution specialist position and create a 1.0 victim witness specialist and 0.5 administrative specialist, leveraging state Chapter 950 reimbursement; (2) Sheriff's office - abolish a senior admin position and create a corrections officer position to address jail staffing needs; (3) Clerk of Courts - reclass an administrative assistant to administrative specialist to manage scheduling duties previously defunded; (4) Medical Examiner - abolish the vacant deputy chief medical examiner (physician) position and create a senior administrative assistant, generating significant cost savings. Medical Examiner Director Jess explained the physician position was unsustainable due to lower-than-projected case volumes, noting the office is building volume gradually with new county and hospital contracts. The committee approved forwarding all positions to HR, Finance and Property.

discussions.item: Marathon County Ordinance 5.09 - Chief Deputy Appointment Update
discussions.body: Sheriff Chad presented an ordinance update required by 2025 Wisconsin Act 196, which merged the chief deputy and under sheriff roles so that the chief deputy automatically assumes the sheriff's duties if needed, and removed the chief deputy position from civil service oversight, making it solely the sheriff's appointment. Corporation Counsel Brian Desmond also recommended removing a provision barring the chief deputy from seeking the office of sheriff, citing both practical concerns about limiting the candidate pool and potential legal issues with restricting access to elective office. The committee approved forwarding the ordinance amendment to the county board.

discussions.item: Non-Lapsing Contingency Account for Medical Examiner's Office
discussions.body: Administrator Leonard proposed creating a non-lapsing contingency account capped at $250,000 for the Medical Examiner's office, funded by year-end operating surpluses rather than levy, to cover volatile revenue years and expensive capital equipment needs such as the $300,000 full-body X-ray (Phobus) machine. Supervisor John Robinson expressed support but raised concerns that the $250,000 cap is high compared to other departments' accounts and that frequent periodic reviews should ensure the funds are not used as a budget workaround. Supervisor Jason raised questions about whether building expenses like roofs would draw from this fund, and Leonard confirmed it could serve as a blended funding source with board approval via supermajority vote. The committee approved forwarding the proposal to the county board.

discussions.item: 6A - Flock Safety ALPR Technology Presentation
discussions.body: Captain Jeff Stefanic of the sheriff's investigations division began an educational presentation on automated license plate reader (ALPR) technology, explaining the sheriff's office has used Flock Safety systems since 2023. He described how stationary cameras capture and read license plates using infrared illumination and character-recognition software, noting the technology is used commercially in toll systems and car washes. The presentation was ongoing at the end of the transcript and covered what the system is, its capabilities, data retention policies, and public safety outcomes, with the stated goal of educating the committee amid public questions generated by recent news coverage.

overview: The Marathon County Public Safety Committee received two informational presentations: a data-driven update on the county's drug treatment court program (2018–2026 year-to-date) and an overview of North Central Health Care's Hope House supportive housing program. No formal votes were taken on substantive matters aside from adjournment. The meeting highlighted that Marathon County's treatment court success rate of 58.8% exceeds the state average of 56.6%, and that lack of supportive housing was identified as the top gap in a recent strategic intercept mapping exercise.

discussions.item: Drug Treatment Court Program Overview and Data Presentation
discussions.body: Justice Programs Coordinator Lori Ari and Data Officer Michael Schultz presented a comprehensive data report on the county's drug treatment court, covering 2018 through August 6, 2026. Schultz used Power BI dashboards connected to the DOJ's CORE system to show referrals, admissions, eligibility breakdowns, days in program, housing and employment status changes, and success rates. A notable highlight was that exactly 100 participants had either graduated, been terminated, or administratively discharged since the program's inception, with Marathon County's 58.8% success rate slightly exceeding the state average of 56.6% for the 2019–2023 period. Ari noted 15 participants have had children returned from out-of-home placement and six drug-free babies have been born to program participants.

discussions.item: Committee Q&A on Treatment Court
discussions.body: Supervisor Jason asked whether graduates stay in contact with the program after completion; Ari explained graduates fill out a questionnaire about desired contact level, are required to check in at court at 30, 60, and 90 days post-graduation, and many continue to volunteer or sponsor new participants. Supervisor Kim asked about the reasons for the 40% termination rate seen in the state comparison data; Ari explained termination typically results from absconding, significant new criminal charges, or long-term failure to show any improvement. A committee member who identified as a former prosecutor noted the visible transformation in participants he had seen at graduations.

discussions.item: 6C: North Central Health Care Hope House Program Overview
discussions.body: Wendy Peterson, Director of Acute Care Services at North Central Health Care, presented an overview of Hope House, a supportive sober-living program operating under the Apricity model with two locations: an eight-bed men's facility in Wausau (average daily census 6.5) and an eight-bed women's facility in Antigo (average daily census 5.5), serving Marathon, Lincoln, and Langlade Counties. Residents must have completed treatment, maintained 30 days of sobriety, and engage in 40 hours per week of work, school, volunteering, or programming. Funding comes from resident rent supplemented by Marathon County cash levy for the Wausau location and Langlade County cash levy for the Antigo facility. County Administrator Jason noted that the recent Strategic Intercept Mapping exercise identified lack of supportive housing as the number-one gap in the community's justice and recovery system.

overview: The Wausau City Council Human Resources Committee met on August 10th and approved two HR-related reclassifications: elevating the HR Specialist position to HR Generalist with a pay increase, and approving a temporary planning intern for the comprehensive plan update. The committee also approved organizational restructuring and succession planning changes for the Department of Public Works and Utilities on a 4-1 vote, over objections from Alderwoman Larson who argued the changes would not address underlying problems in the department.

discussions.item: Approval of Minutes
discussions.body: A motion to approve the minutes of the preceding month was made by Alder Wiskowski and seconded by Alder Kilian. The motion passed on a voice vote with no opposition noted.

discussions.item: Reclassification of Human Resources Specialist to Human Resources Generalist
discussions.body: Interim HR Director Ann Keenan presented the reclassification, explaining that the incumbent (Jennifer) had long been performing generalist-level duties including workforce planning, labor relations, FMLA, compliance, and HRIS administration — well beyond a specialist's narrow scope. Several committee members, including Alder Kilian and Alder Wiskowski, raised concerns about whether the change should wait until a new HR Director was hired, worried that a new director might want to restructure the department differently. Alderwoman Mertens argued the incumbent deserved to be compensated at the level she was already performing. After debate, Keenan argued the reclassification was already part of former director Lisa's vision and that the employee was doing the work regardless of title. The committee ultimately voted to approve the reclassification, which will carry a wage increase and move to the finance committee.

discussions.item: Approval of Creation of Planning Intern Position
discussions.body: Planner Carrie [last name not stated] presented a request for a temporary part-time planning intern, approximately 15 hours per week at roughly $16/hour for about four months, estimated total cost no more than $5,000, funded from already-budgeted comprehensive plan funds. The intern would assist with public engagement data collection and aggregation for the city's comprehensive plan update. Alder Kilian questioned whether the incoming administrative assistant could handle the work, and Alder Wiskowski asked about measurable benefits to the city. Alderwoman Mertens clarified the cost would come from already-allocated comprehensive plan funds — not new budget dollars — which resolved some concerns. The committee approved the position on a voice vote.

discussions.item: Organizational Structure Changes and Succession Planning for Department of Public Works and Utilities
discussions.body: DPW Director Eric Lindman presented proposed reclassifications: building inspector reclassification, fleet manager to fleet superintendent, and traffic maintainers to traffic control specialists. He also proposed eliminating a difficult-to-fill part-time facilities maintenance position and reassigning two equipment operators from streets to report directly under the facilities manager, projecting a net savings of approximately $9,000 per year. Alderwoman Larson opposed the item, arguing it would not address what she described as serious ongoing problems in the DPW department that she said were expected to come before the committee in the future; she moved to table until the next meeting. A point of order was raised and debated. Alder Kilian argued the succession planning was not related to broader departmental issues and supported moving forward. The motion to approve passed 4-1, with Alderwoman Larson casting the dissenting vote.

discussions.item: HR Department Staffing Concerns
discussions.body: Following the DPW vote, Alder Wiskowski raised concerns about the HR department operating with only two staff members while Interim Director Keenan and specialist Jennifer manage an overwhelming workload including firefighter hiring, crossing guard recruitment, benefits expansion, and Workday system administration. Keenan acknowledged the department was 'at critical' staffing levels and noted that one FMLA event would leave them with a single employee. She said she planned to bring a request to the full City Council on Wednesday to accelerate hiring of the HR coordinator position rather than waiting for a new director. The committee encouraged Keenan not to suffer in silence and asked whether a temp hire might help bridge the gap.

discussions.body: A commissioner moved to approve the minutes and received a second. The motion carried without discussion or opposition.

discussions.item: Public Hearing – Rezoning of 4205 and 4307 Weston Avenue (B2 to LI) and Conditional Use Permit for Personal Storage Facility
discussions.body: Staff presenter Jennifer explained that both the comprehensive plan (updated 2024) and the Weston Avenue corridor plan (2022) designate this area for commercial development with B2 and B3 as preferred zoning districts, and that staff recommends against the rezoning to LI. Applicant Steve (last name not fully stated, address 8303 Alderson Street West) argued the corridor has seen no commercial development in the years since the plan was adopted and that the property has had no serious commercial interest in 15 years of his ownership. His engineer Nick from Marathon Technical Services explained the applicant chose LI over B3 due to less stringent landscaping and building material requirements. Dean Dietrich, attorney for the Wausau Child Care Foundation (owner of the adjoining parcel to the east), appeared to note the foundation had no formal position but was interested as an adjoining landowner, and indicated the foundation board would likely be open to selling the property if no major change in childcare funding occurs. Commissioner Joel noted he personally had little objection to storage use given the lack of retail development and proximity to existing LI-zoned land, while staff emphasized the employment objectives of the corridor plan and noted the commission has seen four similar storage facility applications in recent years with mixed results. The commission worked through four determination questions and found the rezoning inconsistent with the comprehensive plan on questions one, two, and three, with a split (approximately 3-2) on question four regarding consistency with surrounding land uses given the adjacent LI zoning. The commission voted 3-2 to recommend denial of the rezoning to the village board.

discussions.item: Motion to Defer Action on Conditional Use Permit – 4205 and 4307 Weston Avenue
discussions.body: Because the property is not currently zoned to allow a personal storage facility, the commission voted to defer action on the conditional use permit pending the village board's decision on the rezoning request. The motion carried without opposition.

discussions.item: Special Exception Sign Permit – LNS Electric, 5707 Scoffeld Avenue
discussions.body: Staff presented a request from LNS Electric to reface an existing freestanding monument sign and add a decorative top element. The proposed sign would be 9 feet tall with an 8-foot setback from the property line; village code requires a setback equal to sign height, triggering the special exception. Staff recommended approval. A commissioner moved to approve and the motion carried unanimously without significant debate.

discussions.item: Animal Fancier License – 5512 North Birch Lane (Lenzo/Bukowski)
discussions.body: The applicant Kira Lenzo (formerly Bukowski) requested a license to keep four dogs for sled dog activities. The village humane officer recommended denial based on insufficient property size relative to the number and size of the dogs. Three public commenters spoke: neighbor Barbara Schultz (1304 [inaudible] Street) supported the license, saying the dogs are not noisy; neighbor Ceda (5604 [inaudible] Lane) opposed it, citing odor from dog waste on a patio area draining toward her yard and an unresolved conflict with the applicant; and Nancy Vet (2306 North 4th Avenue, Wausau), grandmother of the opposing neighbor's children, also opposed, citing smell and the small size of the residence. The commission sided with the humane officer's findings and voted unanimously to recommend denial to the village board.

title: Village Board Meeting
overview: The Kronenwetter Village Board held its August 10, 2026 meeting with six of seven trustees present (Stowell absent/excused). The board approved two significant actions: eliminating the village's oak wilt ordinance and reimbursement policy, and passing a one-year moratorium on new data center development applications to allow planning and utility committees time to study the issue. The meeting also featured extensive financial updates on the village's tax increment districts, equalization values, and upcoming property reassessment process.

discussions.item: Public Comment - Written Submissions
discussions.body: Two written public comments were read into the record. Lamont Yager of Civil Road submitted a lengthy letter requesting enforcement of oak wilt ordinance 389-1 against the owner of 1916 Civil Road, asking police enforcement of 389-2 regarding a dead tree defined as a nuisance, and calling for an investigation of Village President Joling for alleged obstruction of justice, accusing him of being 'petty, tyrannical and vindictive.' President Joling noted that the tree in question is being handled following administrator Deval's contact with the property owner, who is waiting until after August 15th to cut the oak. A second letter was entered into the minutes without being read aloud due to length.

discussions.item: Police Chief Report
discussions.body: The police chief (referred to as 'Terry') reported on several notable incidents: a high number of domestic violence calls in July including one involving ten felony charges and three misdemeanors with a weapon; a 12-year sentence handed down in the Maple Ridge Road aggravated battery case, with the department receiving praise from the district attorney; and a high-speed pursuit of an attempted homicide suspect that came through Kronenwetter at speeds exceeding 120 mph, with KPD participating under their pursuit policy. Trustee Coyle asked about body camera status; the chief confirmed the department has had body cams since approximately 2021-2022, currently using updated units compatible with their in-car systems, with storage through City-County IT rather than higher-cost providers like Axon.

discussions.item: Village Administrator Report
discussions.body: Administrator Deval welcomed new Community Development Director Nathan Samot, who began the previous Thursday. He updated the board on several matters: the Wausau School District superintendent plans to attend the October 12th board meeting to discuss a possible referendum; a meeting is planned with Green Tree regarding the Mortensen International Golf Course area and access issues; a lawsuit by St. Teresa Church over an open pit sand mine decision is pending a new judge after the original recused herself, with the village's attorney suggesting it may be thrown out; and an Act 10 update was referenced with no immediate action planned. Deval also noted that TID 1's prospective distribution center tenant may begin construction as early as September or October.

discussions.item: Revaluation Update - Village Assessor Report
discussions.body: The administrator presented on behalf of the assessor, explaining that letters are being mailed today to all property owners informing them of an upcoming exterior revaluation process beginning the week of August 24th. A field team of five individuals from Associated Appraisal will survey the entire village. Property owners need take no action; the revaluation will affect December 2027 tax bills, not 2026. Assessment values are expected to need to increase on average approximately 40% to reach full value, as the current assessment ratio has fallen to 63%. The village must complete this revaluation by end of 2027 or the state will conduct it at two to three times the cost in 2028.

discussions.item: Finance Director Report
discussions.body: Finance Director John presented preliminary 2027 budget figures from the state. The village's equalized valuation reached nearly $1.2 billion, a $100 million or 9.4% increase, but only $8.8 million is net new construction, meaning the assessment ratio dropped from 69% to 63%. The net new construction limit means the tax levy can technically only increase by about $12,000 for 2027, which does not cover staff raises or basic costs. TID 1 saw a concerning $2.5 million valuation reduction — partly from the local assessor's obsolescence adjustments on two parcels and partly from an unexplained $1.4 million state correction the finance director is still awaiting explanation on — meaning the general fund advance to TID 1 could rise from roughly $125,000 to as much as $200,000 in 2027. On a positive note, the village has $49 million remaining under its general obligation debt limit and still has room under the 12% TID valuation cap, with the finance director flagging a potential future TID 5 to help finance a new water tower.

discussions.body: Trustee Coyle moved and Trustee Mortensen seconded approval of the July 27, 2026 meeting minutes. The motion passed unanimously with no discussion.

discussions.item: Oak Wilt Ordinance Elimination
discussions.body: The board discussed eliminating the village's oak wilt ordinance (389-1) and its associated reimbursement policy, following a unanimous recommendation from the CLIP committee on August 3rd. Key reasons cited included: the reimbursement fund has been depleted for several years, the village has no certified tree inspector on staff or under contract, and oak wilt is so prevalent throughout the village and surrounding municipalities that enforcement is not feasible. Trustee Solheim raised concern about losing the April-through-August pruning restriction window and its value for developers; staff noted the DNR classifies Marathon County in the north zone with a shorter April 15–July 15 restriction. The board agreed that DNR guidelines would be linked on the village website. Trustee Coyle moved and a trustee seconded to eliminate both the ordinance and reimbursement policy; the motion passed unanimously.

discussions.item: Resolution 2026-011 - Temporary Moratorium on New Data Center Development
discussions.body: The board considered a one-year moratorium on new data center development applications, referring the matter to the planning commission and utility committee for study of zoning, utility, infrastructure, and land use implications. Administrator Deval noted there is significant misinformation circulating about data centers and the village simply needs better information before acting on any application. Nathan Samot flagged a minor typographical error in the resolution. Trustee Coyle moved and Trustee Mortensen seconded; the resolution passed 7-0 on a roll call vote. It was noted that Marathon County is considering similar action covering townships, and each municipality must pass its own.

discussions.item: Consideration of Items for Next Agenda
discussions.body: Nathan Samot discussed the appeals process for conditional use permits, stating his research found no villages where CUP appeals go to the village board and recommending the matter be referred to the planning commission, partly because two board members sit on the planning commission, creating impartiality concerns. The board will also receive the 10-year Capital Improvement Plan (CIP) for the first time at the next meeting, after it completes review at the APC. Deval indicated funding mechanisms and affordability analysis will be ready at that time.

title: Regular Meeting
overview: The Wausau School Board held its regular August 10, 2026 meeting, dominated by a lengthy discussion on elementary class sizes prompted by Rib Mountain Elementary parents concerned about a projected 25-student first grade class with no scheduling flexibility as a single-section school. The board also received a referendum construction update showing projects at John Marshall, Rib Mountain, Franklin, and Lincoln near completion, and unanimously approved eight policy updates required by Wisconsin Act 89, a new law governing staff-student communications and mandatory reporting timelines.

discussions.item: Public Comment: Rib Mountain Elementary Class Size
discussions.body: Two speakers addressed class size concerns at Rib Mountain Elementary. Ann Wicklund, a retired Wausau School District director of special education with 50 years in early childhood education, spoke about the developmental importance of K-3 class sizes and the risks of a projected 25-student first grade class, but was cut off slightly over her 3-minute limit. Nate Bartsch, a Rib Mountain parent speaking on behalf of many families present in the audience, argued that as a single-section school Rib Mountain has 'zero flexibility' to balance behavioral or academic needs across classrooms, and asked the board for immediate action for the 2026-27 school year rather than just acknowledgment.

discussions.item: Consent Agenda Approval
discussions.body: Board President Bouché sought a motion to approve the consent agenda covering staff appointments, replacements, contract changes, separations, leaves, retirements, meeting minutes from July 13 and August 3 sessions, payment of bills, budget and investment reports, and donations from Lynn Miller, Nikki O'Neal, and an anonymous donor. The motion was approved, though Bouché acknowledged moving too quickly and noted he heard Vice President Trollop's (participating virtually) vote at the end.

discussions.item: Referendum 2022 Construction Updates - Nexus Presentation
discussions.body: Representatives Chris and Kevin Hickman of Nexus provided updates on construction at John Marshall, Rib Mountain, Franklin, and Lincoln schools, noting occupancy inspections were scheduled for the following week and most classrooms had been turned over for cleaning. Kevin Hickman thanked the district for a 12-year partnership and credited the community-approved referendum with producing 'safer schools, renewed infrastructure, and improving environments.' Board member Pat McKee publicly noted that Nexus president Mike had not appeared before the board since threatening legal action years earlier, calling it a missed opportunity for a 'decent touch,' and asked Hickman to relay that message.

discussions.item: District Class Size Presentation and Discussion
discussions.body: Administration presented current class size guidelines (K-1: max 25; 2-3: max 27; 4-5: max 29; AGR schools K-3: max 18), six years of average class size data showing district average of 20.2 for 2026-27, and modeled an alternative 21-23-25 framework that would require eight additional sections and approximately $1.1 million in staffing costs against a projected $1.36 million budget shortfall for 2027-28. Board members engaged in extensive debate: Pat McKee argued for a 'classroom complexity factor' beyond pure enrollment numbers, drawing applause; Lance Trollop (virtual) pushed back on media framing that class sizes had hit a six-year high, noting the increase was less than one student; Cory Sillars advocated for adding para support to younger grades and requested a school-by-school staffing model; Jennifer Paoli asked about para allocation processes and whether a lower-cost para increase could substitute for new sections; and Nick Crochiere raised the possibility of a future referendum targeted at class size reduction. Administration confirmed Rib Mountain first grade would receive an enrollment para given its enrollment at the maximum, and noted the district is already approximately 40 staff short with two weeks until school starts.

discussions.item: Act 89 Policy Review and Approval
discussions.body: District administrator Tabitha Gundrum (identified as Ms. Gundrum/Mensley in transcript) walked the board through eight updated or new policies required by Wisconsin Act 89, passed in March 2026, covering staff-student communication standards, annual training requirements, and mandatory reporting timelines. Key changes include a statutory prohibition on direct staff-to-student personal device communication, with SportsYou and Google Chat identified as approved platforms; removal of 'preferential treatment' language from policies as unenforceable; new 'grooming' definition sections; and strict reporting deadlines requiring parent notification by 5:00 p.m. the same day if a report is received before end of school day, or by noon the next calendar day if received after hours. Gundrum noted training launched August 1 with a 25-minute attorney-produced video, with roughly 30% of staff already completing it, and that volunteer training remains a significant logistical challenge. The board voted unanimously to approve all eight policy changes.

discussions.item: Legislative Liaison Update and CESA 9 Report
discussions.body: Cory Sillars reported on the CESA 9 annual convention held August 3, noting he chaired the meeting in the absence of regular chair Chris Petronek, that a new member from the Lakeland area joined, and that Larry Schaefer of DC Everest was recognized for 30 years of service. Sillars also mentioned speaking with Secretary Duffy over the weekend about construction costs and energy prices. Superintendent Bushman thanked Rib Mountain families for attending, announced the August 24 staff welcome-back event, and invited board members to attend.

Ann Wicklund, 227-350 Bard Owl Avenue, Wausau, a retired Wausau School District director of special education with over 50 years in early childhood education, raised concerns about a projected 25-student first grade class at Rib Mountain Elementary and the importance of class size in early childhood development; she was cut off slightly over the 3-minute limit. Nate Bartsch, 151306 Kingfisher Lane, Rib Mountain, spoke on behalf of many Rib Mountain families present in the audience, arguing the school's single-section structure leaves no flexibility to manage behavioral or academic complexity and asking the board for concrete action for the 2026-27 school year. A third potential speaker, Jess Bartz, declined to speak.

discussions.body: The committee reached consensus not to accept the New Heights proposal for property redevelopment at this time. The chair summarized that administration would communicate with New Heights regarding additional information requirements and that the property would remain open for redevelopment. New Heights could return to the agenda once additional information was provided. The committee then adjourned, with a motion moved and seconded by Hart, approved unanimously.

discussions.item: 2027 Budget Development - Rates, Fees, and Revenue Update
discussions.body: County Administrator Lance Leonard reported that the Department of Revenue released preliminary net new construction numbers at 1.54%, roughly 10% below the county's budget projection of 1.65%, meaning less revenue than anticipated. Staff circulated spreadsheets to department heads with a built-in 3% fee increase assumption, asking them to flag statutory limitations, areas where 3% doesn't cover costs, and fees where business reasons argue against increases. Leonard noted that unlike private businesses, county government cannot charge more than the cost of service delivery. A supervisor asked how child care ranked in the budget prioritization exercise, and Leonard said the $50,000 child care continuation proposal ranked highest among all new discretionary projects.

discussions.item: Marshfield Area Chamber of Commerce Partnership Request - $25,000
discussions.body: Denise Sam, executive director of the Marshfield Area Chamber of Commerce and Industry, presented the chamber's work serving a 10-15 mile radius including Marathon County communities like Stratford, Spencer, and Rozellville, and requested $25,000 annually matching what Wood County provides. Supervisor Krums questioned how many other chambers serve Marathon County and whether the county contributes to any of them; Administrator Leonard noted the county is a member of Greater Wausau Chamber and that the airport belongs to the Mosinee chamber, but the county does not provide economic development funds to chambers. A supervisor raised concerns about redundancy with MCDEVCO and the county's limited discretionary spending, stating objection to the request. MCDEVCO Executive Director Kim Weber suggested the better path was a referral relationship rather than separate funding. Because the item was listed as an educational presentation, no action could be taken.

discussions.item: MCDEVCO Monthly Report
discussions.body: MCDEVCO Executive Director Kim Weber reported that all $1 million of the Marathon County Revolving Loan Fund has been deployed into the community, with $962,000 dispersed last year. She highlighted loan recipients including Redwood Street Roasters in Edgar ($250,000), Sugar 'n Spice Cheesecakes, Peking Restaurant, and The Story Seller. The Pelzer Revolving Loan Fund for low-income rural septic system replacement has assisted over 17 systems with $256,000 disbursed and $250,000 remaining. The Wausau Business Incubator is 92% full across office, manufacturing, and kitchen spaces. Weber noted upcoming programming including an accounting workshop in partnership with NTC and UWSP and a personal financial statement lunch and learn with the Wausau River District.

discussions.item: Child Caring Scholarship Program Update and $50,000 Continuation Proposal
discussions.body: Kelly from Child Caring reported that of the 30 scholarships funded by the county's $200,000 American Rescue Plan Act allocation (contracted October 2024, starting January 2025), 22 have been awarded and 20 individuals have completed training and been job-placed in child care settings, supporting approximately 350 children. Eight scholarships remain and three people are already enrolled in a new class. A proposed $50,000 continuation would fund 10 additional teachers at $4,000 each ($40,000 in scholarships, $10,000 to Child Caring for administration), and Child Caring has separately submitted a $50,000 grant request to the Women's Fund through the Community Foundation to potentially match county funds and support 20 total new teachers. Supervisor Lamers and Chair Gibbs expressed strong support. The loss of Child Care Counts subsidy funding at end of June—potentially millions of dollars in Marathon County—has already caused six programs and 60 slots to close in the last three months, with 15-20% cost increases to families anticipated.

discussions.body: Extension staff reported participation in Farm Technology Days in Stratford in early July and the ongoing Marathon County Fair. Horticulture Educator Janelle Ware described an upcoming multi-disciplinary local officials workshop focused on nature-based solutions to reduce weather-related impacts and costs, designed as a networking event to connect government agencies across departments and disciplines so that low-cost mitigation opportunities can be acted on more effectively.
