overview: The Marathon County Infrastructure Committee met to approve several infrastructure and budget items, including a new four-way stop at County Trunk X and Tesh Lane/Turbani Drive, a resolution supporting changes to state trucking restrictions on Business 51, an amendment to the 2026 budget for LRIP funding, and authorization to proceed with design finalization and bidding for a new Marathon County highway shop. The highway shop financing discussion was particularly significant, with staff presenting a strategy to use existing low-interest debt and North Central Healthcare revenues to minimize new borrowing costs to taxpayers on what is currently estimated as a roughly $50 million project.

discussions.item: Approval of June/July 2, 2026 Meeting Minutes
discussions.body: Chair Gibbs called for a motion to approve the minutes. A motion was made by Gregor and seconded by Sterber; Gibbs initially missed Coyle's involvement and apologized. The motion carried unanimously on a voice vote.

discussions.item: 2027 Budget Development - Fee Schedule and New Positions
discussions.body: Staff (identified as Mr. Leonard, the county administrator) reported that departments have been circulated the existing fee schedule following the board's direction to apply a standard 3% fee increase, with exceptions being reviewed for statutory limits, areas where costs have not risen, and market-sensitive services like solid waste. Leonard also reported no new position requests or reclassifications were submitted for departments under the Infrastructure Committee's jurisdiction. Chair Gibbs noted that three resolutions from the ERC committee may bring future cost and staffing implications and asked that those be considered during the budget process.

discussions.item: Four-Way Stop at County Trunk X / Tesh Lane / Turbani Drive
discussions.body: Highway Commissioner Kevin presented a traffic study by EMCS showing the intersection met crash warrant criteria (exceeding five crashes in a one-month period), with a majority being right-angle crashes, which are among the most severe. Volume warrants were close to being met, and a speed study was expected to confirm the reduced threshold would apply at the 35 mph posted limit. The Village of Rothschild had previously recommended against stopping major traffic on Double X but lacked crash data at the time; the Village of Kronenwetter had not yet responded. Kevin recommended converting to a four-way stop. Supervisor Kelly moved to recommend the county board modify Section 7.04(6) of the Marathon County Code of Ordinances to create a four-way stop; Chair Gibbs amended the motion to include flashing stop signs on County Trunk X at the committee's request. The motion carried unanimously.

discussions.item: Resolution Supporting Modification of Trans 276.065 Trucking Restrictions on Business 51
discussions.body: Kevin explained that the existing state restriction prohibiting trucks over 65 feet on Business 51 from I-39 to US-51 near Highway K is unenforced and inconsistent with actual use by businesses like Domar Tile using standard 53-foot semi-trailers. Supervisor Coyle moved to recommend the county board support a resolution encouraging the state to modify Trans 276 to allow vehicles exceeding 65 feet on Business 51 from the Rothschild exit up to and including the Highway 29 exit, expanding the original scope. Supervisor Griner questioned whether the limit should extend further north to I-39/51, but Kevin noted uncertainty about downtown Wausau street capacity. The motion was seconded by Griner and carried unanimously.

discussions.item: Amendment to 2026 Budget for LRIP Funding - Highway E
discussions.body: Kevin explained that an unusual pavement failure on Highway E north of Marshfield — where the lower asphalt layer stripped and failed rapidly — forced the project into the 2026 paving program ahead of schedule. LRIP funds from future years were applied to offset costs, but because the decision was made after the budget cycle, those revenues need to be added to the current year budget. Supervisor She moved to approve the budget amendment; Supervisor Griner seconded. The motion carried unanimously on a voice vote.

discussions.item: Marathon County Highway Shop Construction - Funding Mechanism and Project Authorization
discussions.body: Administrator Leonard and Finance Director Sam Fensky presented a detailed financing strategy for the new highway shop, estimated at approximately $50 million (with the actual figure expected to differ). The county has $30 million in highway fund reserves designated for the project. Staff proposed avoiding new long-term debt by instead transitioning existing low-interest debt (issued 2019-2022 at roughly 2% for Lake View campus renovations) currently serviced by North Central Healthcare revenues onto the general debt levy, and redirecting those North Central revenues (ramping from $3 million to $4.1 million annually) to fund the highway shop — saving an estimated $25 million in interest compared to issuing new debt at current 4-5% rates. Chris presented project design progress, noting the design is 90-100% complete, coordinated burns of demolished homes on the Kronenwetter site have been completed with the fire department, and bids are targeted for September with a guaranteed maximum price and final county board approval expected by mid-October. Construction would begin in earnest in spring 2027 due to 10-12 month lead times for pre-cast concrete panels. Geothermal HVAC and enhanced insulation were cited as energy efficiency strategies. Supervisor Griner moved to authorize staff to proceed with phase three construction and finalize construction documents for bidding; Supervisor Coyle seconded. The motion carried unanimously.

discussions.item: NOTIP Program 2027-2030 Chapter Five - MPO Projects Discussion
discussions.body: Chair Gibbs walked through projects in the Metropolitan Planning Organization's long-range plan, including the Evergreen-Decatur Wisconsin River crossing in Wausau, the Bridge Street bridge widening, County Trunk Highway O river crossing to Highway NN, the Oman bridge in Schofield over the Eau Claire River, Military Road Wisconsin River crossing, Gardner Park Road in Kronenwetter, County Trunk Highway X to Sandy Lane in Weston, the Kowalski Road interchange, and the Ryan Street interchange at Highway 29 in Weston. Supervisor Robertson cautioned that many of these are long-standing wish-list items requiring community-led studies and environmental review before advancing, citing the Kowalski Road interchange as an example that keeps being listed without completing required preliminary steps. Kevin emphasized that purpose-and-need justification and environmental impacts — especially wetlands and floodplains along the Wisconsin River — are major hurdles for any new crossings. Administrator Leonard suggested inviting MPO planner Lori Kimmons to a future meeting to provide an overview as those discussions develop, which the committee agreed was a good idea.

discussions.body: Supervisor Robertson noted that at the last executive committee meeting, a discussion was held about Bug Tussle's failure to complete the committed southern fiber loop. A joint meeting between the Infrastructure Committee and the HR, Finance and Property Committee will be scheduled to evaluate next steps regarding the county's agreement with Bug Tussle.

overview: Marathon County's Joint Extension, Education & Economic Development Committee and Human Resources, Finance & Property Committee held a joint meeting to hear a proposal from New Heights Climbing and Fitness co-founder Tia Koval requesting transfer of three River Drive properties (210, 212, and 326 River Drive) for $1 in exchange for an estimated $6 million private investment to create a climbing gym, fitness center, and event venue. After the presentation, public comment, and extensive questioning about the business plan, financing, and competitive market, both committees voted to go into closed session to discuss negotiation strategies for the River Drive properties and divestment of the Thomas Street property.

discussions.item: Approval of June 4th, 2026 Meeting Minutes
discussions.body: A motion was made and seconded by Vice Chair Cavalli to approve the minutes of the June 4th, 2026 Extension Education and Economic Development Committee meeting. The motion passed on a voice vote with no discussion.

discussions.item: New Heights Climbing and Fitness River Drive Proposal Presentation
discussions.body: Co-founder Tia Koval presented a proposal requesting the $1 transfer of 210, 212, and 326 River Drive from Marathon County in exchange for a projected $6 million private investment. The plan includes a bouldering and rope climbing gym, a 24-hour fitness center, the Ethos event venue, and co-working space, with full operations projected by Q4 2027. Koval said the project is primarily financed through an SBA loan with Incredible Bank, supplemented by private equity, potential TIF assistance from the City of Wausau, and WEDC grants. EBITDA projections range from $361,000 in Year 1 to $1.28 million in Year 5.

discussions.item: Committee Questions on Financing and Business Plan
discussions.body: Supervisors raised significant questions about the proposal's financial details. One supervisor asked why EBITDA rather than net income was used in projections and whether capital expenditure plans were complete. Supervisor Nice requested a comprehensive business plan, feasibility study with demographics, detailed financial statements, and preliminary construction plans. Chair Kennedy noted that operating expenses appeared to increase only 1.6% over four years while revenue nearly doubled, calling the figures questionable. Supervisor Krems asked whether Koval would object if a competing facility later sought similar county assistance; Koval said she did not think Wausau's population could support more than one climbing gym. Koval acknowledged that TIF financing had not been advanced due to the lack of a confirmed location, and that committed private investors exist but were not named in the business plan.

discussions.item: Public Comment — Kim Winterhoff
discussions.body: Kim Winterhoff, a local business owner and real estate investor, spoke in strong support of the proposal. She argued the facility should be viewed as a long-term economic anchor and community center rather than just a rock climbing gym, citing demand from Central Wisconsin residents who currently drive to Appleton or Green Bay to climb. She vouched personally for Tia Koval and Steve Arnold's craftsmanship and business competence, and urged the committee to consider long-term tourism revenue, workforce retention, and youth programming benefits rather than treating the property transfer as a simple asset transaction.

discussions.item: RFP Process and Property Divestment Discussion
discussions.body: County staff Chris [Holman] confirmed the RFP was issued April 23rd with a July due date, drew approximately six attendees at the first walk-through, and received only one formal proposal — from New Heights. Outreach included press releases, radio interviews, online posting, and emails to approximately 40 developers. Supervisor Naxer confirmed this was the first RFP issued for these properties. Supervisor Michael raised concerns about the county's obligation to maximize taxpayer return, while county administration explained that the RFP process was designed to evaluate broader community benefit criteria rather than highest dollar value, consistent with direction the board had previously provided. County Administrator Leonard noted that the manner in which properties were acquired can dictate how they are sold, and that closed session was appropriate to discuss negotiation strategy.

discussions.item: Motion to Go Into Closed Session
discussions.body: Board Chair Kurt Gibbs moved to go into closed session under Wisconsin Statute 19.85(1)(e) for competitive or bargaining reasons, to discuss strategies for negotiating a River Drive property contract and divestment of the Thomas Street property. Both the HR Finance & Property Committee and the Extension Education & Economic Development Committee voted separately by roll call to enter closed session. Online supervisors were informed they would be placed in a lobby until the closed session concluded.

publicComment: One speaker offered public comment. Kim Winterhoff, a local business owner and real estate investor, spoke in favor of the New Heights proposal. She argued Wausau lacks year-round indoor recreation options, that Central Wisconsin residents already drive long distances to climb, and that the facility would serve as a tourism anchor and youth destination. She personally vouched for the quality and competence of proposers Tia Koval and Steve Arnold, and urged the committee to evaluate the proposal on long-term community value rather than short-term asset transaction terms.

title: Environmental Resources Committee Meeting
overview: The Marathon County Environmental Resources Committee held its August 4, 2026 meeting and took action on several zoning matters, including approving recommendations on two rezoning petitions, advancing an updated battery energy storage systems ordinance (with an amendment increasing residential setback to 300 feet), approving a 12-month moratorium on data centers in county-zoned towns, and beginning discussion of a new large electric generating facilities ordinance. A notable announcement opened the meeting: the City of Marshfield voluntarily withdrew a rezoning request related to solar because the county's solar ordinance is more restrictive than state law, which prohibits counties from requiring a rezone for solar projects.

discussions.item: Marshfield Solar Rezoning Withdrawal Announcement
discussions.body: Chair Ritter announced before public comment that the City of Marshfield voluntarily withdrew its request to rezone from rural estate to general agriculture. The withdrawal stems from Marathon County's solar ordinance being more restrictive than state law, which does not permit counties to require a rezone for solar projects. Corporation counsel's determination will be added to the packet for committee review, and the item was removed from the agenda.

discussions.item: Public Comment
discussions.body: Six speakers addressed the committee during general public comment, with the majority supporting a moratorium on hyperscale data centers and expressing support for commercial solar and wind energy development. Speakers cited climate change, water resource protection, grid resilience, and public health concerns. One speaker, Jay Caldwell, argued that 'people don't need data centers — billionaires need data centers to control us,' while others like Dan Barth and Jean Abreu framed renewable energy support in economic and environmental terms. Nikki Cottrell, speaking online, urged the committee to place industrial-scale wind development on a future agenda and adopt a moratorium pending independent environmental review.

discussions.item: 5A1: J Good Rezoning - Farmland Preservation to Rural Estate and General Agriculture, Town of Brighton
discussions.body: Staff member Garrett Pagel presented the staff report recommending approval of the rezone of approximately 37.68 acres — 5 acres to rural estate and 32.68 acres to general agriculture — at the intersection of State Highway 153 and County Road F. The Town of Brighton recommended approval on June 12, 2026. Supervisor Griesbach asked about churches as permitted uses in rural estate zoning and was told churches are a permitted use in that district. No public testimony was offered for, against, or as interested. The committee voted to approve and recommend to the County Board.

discussions.item: 5A2: Weinkauf Rezoning - General Agriculture to Rural Residential, Town of Gunther
discussions.body: Staff presented the rezone request for a parcel at the corner of Duberstein Road and Whiz Road. Supervisor Drewek raised a concern that the Town of Gunther's resolution did not have any written answers to the required questions on page 30, noting it could set a bad precedent. Staff confirmed the town had approved the rezone but left the resolution incomplete. The committee agreed to send the application back to the town to properly complete the resolution before placing it on a future ERC agenda. The public hearing was completed with no public testimony before the motion was made.

discussions.item: 5A4: Battery Energy Storage Systems Ordinance Amendment
discussions.body: Staff Chad Harvey presented updates to the existing battery energy storage ordinance, including clearer hazard mitigation and emergency response plan requirements, a minimum 7-foot fence height, first responder training obligations for commercial systems, 24/7 monitoring requirements, and refined decommissioning provisions. Public testimony from Town of Easton Chairman Dean Beck raised concerns about volunteer fire department capacity, water availability for firefighting lithium battery fires, and groundwater contamination risk. Another speaker questioned whether setbacks of 100-200 feet were adequate given fire risks. Supervisor Drewek moved and Supervisor Kurth seconded an amendment to increase the residential setback for commercial battery systems from 200 feet to 300 feet. The amendment passed with at least one 'no' vote (not unanimous). The full amended ordinance was then moved to the County Board by Supervisor Lemmer, seconded by Supervisor Kurth, and approved.

discussions.item: 5A5: Data Center Moratorium Ordinance
discussions.body: Staff presented a proposed 12-month moratorium on new data center development in county-zoned towns to allow time to research and develop a comprehensive data center ordinance. Chair Ritter and Chair Gibbs clarified the moratorium applies only to the 18 county-zoned towns, not cities, villages, or other towns. Staff proposed an amendment to close a potential loophole by applying the 5,000-square-foot accessory use exemption on a cumulative basis per parcel. The City of Marshfield rezone withdrawal was noted as context. Supervisor Coggs noted 64 data centers already exist in Wisconsin, with large ones in Pleasant Prairie, Port Washington, and a project near Beaver Dam/Dodgeville, and urged careful size-differentiated research during the moratorium. The committee approved the staff-proposed amendment and then approved the moratorium as amended.

discussions.item: 5A6: Large Electric Generating Facilities Ordinance
discussions.body: Staff introduced a new ordinance — described as among the first of its kind in Wisconsin — requiring large electric generating facility developers to submit to the county the same engineering plans submitted to the Public Service Commission, within 30 days of filing with the PSC, for projects in county-zoned towns. Corporation counsel clarified the ordinance cannot compel developers to comply but creates a framework to open dialogue and inform county decision-making about whether to intervene in PSC proceedings or negotiate agreements. Supervisor Drewek asked why the review window was 30 rather than 60 days; Supervisor Lemmer suggested 45 days. Staff acknowledged the 30-day timeline is challenging and that outside expertise may be needed to review engineering documents. No votes on this item were captured in the transcript.

publicComment: Six speakers offered public comment before the public hearing portion. Dan Barth (Town of Knowlton) spoke in favor of the data center moratorium and in support of commercial solar and wind, citing personal observations of climate change over 40 years. Kathy Conley Barth (Mosinee) opposed data centers citing water and energy demands and supported renewable energy. Jean Abreu (Wausau) supported the data center moratorium and commercial-scale renewable energy with county oversight agreements. Jonathan Smith (Wausau, online) supported the moratorium and renewables, citing the committee's strategic plan objectives on groundwater protection. Nikki Cottrell (Brighton Township, online) urged the committee to also place industrial-scale wind development under a moratorium pending independent environmental review, referencing acoustic assessment concerns and wildlife habitat fragmentation. Jay Caldwell (Wausau) supported the data center moratorium and battery storage ordinance while emphasizing public health harms of fossil fuels. Additional residents spoke during individual public hearings: Town of Easton Chairman Dean Beck raised fire safety and water supply concerns about battery storage; Heidi Pesky (Town of McMillan) questioned the adequacy of setbacks for battery fires; Kathy Conley Barth spoke again on battery storage scale; Peggy Koos raised groundwater protection concerns related to data centers.

discussions.body: A resident (Jim) noted during public comment that the minutes incorrectly showed 'yes' under 'present' for vacant committee seats. The mover modified the motion to approve minutes with that correction removed. The motion passed unanimously.

discussions.item: Code Enforcement Update
discussions.body: Building Inspector Roman Magcguire and Planning Director Jennifer Higgins reported on aging cases, noting 26 open complaints in July with 13 already closed. Specific discussion covered the Newport Avenue chronic hoarding property (cleaned up for the fourth time in eight years, with six citations issued this cycle), a 2021 Ross Avenue junkyard case complicated by the property owner's death and her dementia, and the West Marketplace at 4020 Scoffield Avenue where dumpster enclosure violations have been open nearly two years with little visible progress. The police chief noted the SRO partnership has been productive. Committee members asked about citation payment rates and whether escalating bond amounts could deter repeat violators; staff agreed to pull court citation data for the next meeting. The committee also discussed notification letter timing issues given mail now routing through Green Bay.

discussions.item: SAFER Fire Department Update
discussions.body: The SAFER chief reported the board declined to hire six requested personnel, opting instead to explore three positions. The chief emphasized frustration over the ISO rating impact: residents living within five miles of a fire station but more than 1,000 feet from a hydrant are seeing insurance increases of $700–$800, far exceeding the roughly $50 annual tax increase that a failed referendum would have cost. The chief noted the town of Weston considered leaving the district over insurance complaints but appears unlikely to do so after a recent meeting. The lost 'water haul credit' was identified as the key ISO rating driver.

discussions.item: Mountain Bay Metro Police Department Update
discussions.body: The police chief reported the K9 raffle is scheduled for September 12th at Klux, and Monster Bash is October 9th at DC Everest Middle School, with $12,000 in donations already secured. The chief also noted the new police building came in under budget, and an intergovernmental agreement between Rothschild and Weston is expected within a month. A crisis response training was held at the middle school the prior week.

discussions.item: Overnight Parking Regulations – Section 82.107
discussions.body: Public Works Director Michael Wolski proposed adding signage on specific problem streets for daytime/alternating parking restrictions to aid snow plowing, in addition to a village-wide overnight ban aligned with neighboring municipalities (2 a.m. to 6 or 7 a.m.). The police chief pushed back on a patchwork approach, arguing uniform rules are easier to enforce and that officers struggle with varying ordinances across municipalities. Committee members raised concerns about criteria for placing streets on the restricted list, signage costs (estimated roughly $100 per street), and equitable treatment of residents. The committee reached consensus to table the issue to the September 8th meeting, directing staff to return with cost estimates and clear criteria for street selection.

discussions.item: Amendment to Section 50.103 – Nuisance Abatement Storage and Disposal (Ordinance 26-013)
discussions.body: Jennifer Higgins presented the amendment to formalize a 30-day property retention period for items seized during non-summary nuisance abatements, allow immediate disposal of obvious garbage with no apparent value, and enable surplus sale of items of value unclaimed after 30 days. The amendment was prompted by the Newport Avenue cleanup where three dumpsters of material are currently being held at village expense. A committee member raised the question of when seized property legally becomes village possession, particularly given the property owner had attempted to retrieve items during the cleanup. The motion to recommend Ordinance 26-013 passed unanimously and advances to the village board.

discussions.item: Amendment to Section 10.123 – Animal Fanciers (Ordinance 26-014)
discussions.body: Higgins explained that an animal fancier license application triggered a review revealing the Plan Commission no longer needs to be involved under the current zoning code, and that this committee is better suited to handle licensing. The amended ordinance shifts the hearing process to this committee, with humane officers providing recommendations. Trustee Brent Olson raised concern about the lack of an appeal mechanism short of circuit court; staff and the village attorney noted no other appeal body exists, and Olson was encouraged to raise the issue at the village board level. The Plan Commission will hear one pending application next week before the ordinance takes effect. The motion to recommend Ordinance 26-014 to the village board for its August 17th meeting passed, with one audible 'nay' vote noted.

discussions.item: Electric Scooter/E-Moto Ordinance Discussion
discussions.body: The committee discussed two resident emails from young athletes who use scooters to get to practice, and broader community feedback including a petition. The police chief expressed strong skepticism, noting e-motos traveling at high speeds, riders fleeing officers (including a pursuit that evening), and groups of masked riders gathering in parking lots. He argued the village may be leading the state on e-moto regulation and cautioned against following other municipalities' models without careful consideration of speed classification and enforcement practicality. A committee member flagged that an attorney-resident suggested the current e-moto definition may inadvertently include fully electric cars like Teslas; staff agreed to research clarifying language. The committee decided not to change the existing ordinance at this time, directed staff to draft language clarifying that licensed motor vehicles are excluded, and discussed possibly publicizing the issue for public input at the September meeting.

publicComment: One speaker, Jim (address given as 52nd Street), offered public comment. He raised three issues: (1) a correction to meeting minutes showing 'yes' for vacant seats, suggesting dashes instead; (2) concerns about aging code enforcement cases, specifically the nearly two-year-old complaint at 4020 Scoffield Avenue (West Marketplace) involving dumpster enclosure violations, calling for accountability and transparency; and (3) questions about enforcement of the e-moto/scooter ordinance, including how officers would audit speed or wattage specs, and whether the ordinance could inadvertently restrict street-legal electric motorcycles like the Harley-Davidson LiveWire.
